rules.rule: Keep each major type of content in its own main (top-level) directory. Plex's scanners and metadata agents work best when major content types are separated from each other, and Plex strongly recommends in particular that movie and television content live in separate main directories; the article's example gives music its own directory too (/Media/Movies, /Media/Music, /Media/TV Shows). Failing to separate content such as movies and TV shows may result in unexpected or incorrect behavior, not only incorrect matching.
examples:
/Media
   /Movies
      movie content
   /Music
      music content
   /TV Shows
      television content

rules.rule: To collapse several files into one movie library item, give every file the same "MovieName (Release Year)" prefix and distinguish them with trailing text: MovieName (Release Year) - ArbitraryText.ext, that is the title, one space, the release year in round parentheses (shown as "(1994)"; the page does not state a digit count), then a space-hyphen-space separator " - ", then any distinguishing text, then the real file extension ("Some operating systems such as Windows may hide your file extensions by default"). ArbitraryText is "any text useful to you to identify the media from outside Plex" and is never shown in the UI ("The text you have there is not displayed"); Plex displays the actual resolution instead. The page's example places all versions of a title together in one movie folder, /Movies/Pulp Fiction (1994)/ containing "Pulp Fiction (1994) - 1080p.mkv" and "Pulp Fiction (1994) - SD.m4v", so follow that layout, while noting the page does not state co-location as an explicit requirement. Treat " - " as the documented separator rather than an exact requirement: the same page's Editions FAQ merges versions named with dots instead, "Blade Runner (1982).1080p.h264 {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4" and "Blade Runner (1982).4k.hevc {edition-Director's Cut}.mkv". Versions are the same release at different resolutions or encodings; different cuts are Editions and use the {edition-...} suffix instead. Caveat from the page: "Not all Plex apps will allow you to manually choose which version to play. You should not rely on a choice being presented."

In multi-version movie filenames of the form "MovieName (Release Year) - ArbitraryText.ext", the ArbitraryText segment is free-form: per Plex, it "can be any text useful to you to identify the media from outside Plex", and "The text you have there is not displayed." Versions only collapse into one library item when every file shares an identical "MovieName (Release Year)" prefix and sits in the same movie folder (for example /Movies/Pulp Fiction (1994)/ holding "Pulp Fiction (1994) - 1080p.mkv" and "Pulp Fiction (1994) - SD.m4v"); ArbitraryText is the only part that differs. Plex reports quality itself: it "will show you the actual resolution of the media if the app you're using shows you a list", and picks the best file automatically for a mobile app, so labels such as "- 1080p", "- SD", or "- phone" / "- tablet" are for your own benefit outside Plex and carry no meaning to Plex. Do not use ArbitraryText to convey anything Plex is meant to act on. Note that "not displayed" is not the same as "not parsed": the same article's FAQ shows a {edition-...} token inside the filename ("Blade Runner (1982).1080p.h264 {edition-Director's Cut}.mkv") that Plex does read, so a different theatrical release, cut, or 2D-vs-3D variant belongs in an Edition tag, not in ArbitraryText. That FAQ example also separates its version text with dots rather than " - ", so the " - " in the template is the documented form rather than a strict requirement. Source last modified 2022-08-22.
examples: any other label such as '- phone' or '- tablet'

rules.rule: In the pattern "MovieName (Release Year) - ArbitraryText.ext", ".ext" is a placeholder for the file's actual extension, never a literal string, so a renamer must preserve the source file's own extension. Versions of the same movie are merged on the identical "MovieName (Release Year)" prefix, not on the extension, so different versions may carry different extensions: the page shows "Pulp Fiction (1994) - 1080p.mkv" alongside "Pulp Fiction (1994) - SD.m4v", and the Blade Runner edition example mixes .mp4 and .mkv within one edition. Extensions attested on the page: .mkv, .m4v, .mp4.

Classify by what differs. If the files are the same release and differ only in resolution, encoding/codec or container (1080p vs 480p, HEVC vs H.264, MP4 vs MKV), they are versions: put them in the movie folder named "MovieName (Release Year) - ArbitraryText.ext" (e.g. "Pulp Fiction (1994) - 1080p.mkv", "Pulp Fiction (1994) - SD.m4v"); Plex collapses them into one library item and the ArbitraryText is never displayed. If the files are different releases or cuts of the movie (theatrical vs Special Edition, Theatrical vs Director's Cut vs Final Cut, and also 2D vs 3D), they are editions and must be distinguished by the {edition-...} tag, not by version naming. The two are not exclusive: one edition can hold several versions. In that combined case Plex's own example puts each edition in its own folder carrying the tag and repeats the tag in every filename, with the version differentiator written as dot-separated text before it, e.g. /Blade Runner (1982)/Blade Runner (1982).mp4 alongside /Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Director's Cut}/Blade Runner (1982).1080p.h264 {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4 and ....4k.hevc {edition-Director's Cut}.mkv. Set the edition through file naming rather than by editing the movie info in the web app.
examples: versions: 1080p vs 480p, HEVC vs H.264, MP4 vs MKV
editions: Theatrical vs Director's Cut vs Final Cut; 2D vs 3D

rules.rule: An edition is marked with the literal token {edition-<Edition Name>}: an opening curly brace, the lowercase word "edition", exactly one hyphen with no space on either side, the edition name, and a closing curly brace. The edition name may contain spaces and apostrophes; the page's only example is {edition-Director's Cut}, written with a straight ASCII apostrophe (U+0027), not a typographic one. In the page's example the token sits at the end of the name, separated from the preceding text by a single space, and comes before the file extension on files: "Blade Runner (1982).1080p.h264 {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4". The tag is repeated on every file belonging to that edition and also on the containing folder ("/Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Director's Cut}"), and the page states the edition must be set this way ("use the file naming method and not just edit the movie information in the web app"). Scope caveat: this page states no syntax rule in prose, it only shows one worked example, so case-sensitivity of "edition" and any restrictions on characters in the edition name are not documented here and must be confirmed from another source.

To combine editions and versions, put each edition in its own folder under /Movies: the original release in "MovieName (Year)" with no tag, and every other edition in "MovieName (Year) {edition-Name}". The page's stated requirement is on the files rather than the folders: each version file belonging to an edition must itself carry the edition tag, and setting the edition in the web app instead is explicitly not sufficient. In each filename the "{edition-Name}" tag comes last, preceded by exactly one space and immediately followed by the extension, with the version-distinguishing text sitting between the year and the tag. The page's example appends that version text with a dot (Blade Runner (1982).1080p.h264 {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4), while the same page's plain multi-version convention writes it as "MovieName (Release Year) - ArbitraryText.ext"; the page does not reconcile the two, so treat the separator before the version text as unconstrained. Use a plain ASCII apostrophe inside the tag (Director's Cut), as the page's example does.

When a movie edition has multiple versions (same edition, different quality or format), declare the edition through naming rather than by editing the movie information in Plex Web. Plex's guidance: "You'll need to make sure that each of the versions of the edition have the appropriate file naming to specify that edition" and "use the file naming method and not just edit the movie information in the web app." Apply the {edition-Name} tag to the edition's folder AND to every version file inside it; the untagged release stays in the plain movie folder. Per the source example: /Movies/Blade Runner (1982)/Blade Runner (1982).mp4 alongside /Movies/Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Director's Cut}/ containing Blade Runner (1982).1080p.h264 {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4, Blade Runner (1982).1080p.hevc {edition-Director's Cut}.mkv, Blade Runner (1982).4k.h264 {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4 and Blade Runner (1982).4k.hevc {edition-Director's Cut}.mkv. Editing the edition field in the web app may supplement this but does not replace it.
examples: Blade Runner (1982).1080p.h264 {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4 rather than setting the edition field in Plex Web

rules.rule: Do not depend on the viewer hand-picking a version. Files merged as versions (same movie, same release, different resolution or encoding, named MovieName (Release Year) - ArbitraryText.ext) collapse into a single library item, and on playback a Plex app "will automatically request and play the most suitable item by default". Many apps expose a Play Version action, but per the page's Note, "Not all Plex apps will allow you to manually choose which version to play. You should not rely on a choice being presented." Practical consequences: (a) every file you group as a version must be an acceptable thing to play unattended, since you cannot control or override which one a given app picks and there is no default-version setting; (b) the ArbitraryText in the filename is for your own identification outside Plex only, it "is not displayed", so do not use it to label a version for the viewer (apps show the actual resolution instead); (c) if the files are genuinely different cuts rather than different encodes, they are Editions, not Versions, so name them with the {edition-...} tag to get separately selectable items instead of one auto-picked file.
examples: make the version Plex would auto-pick the one you actually want as the default

rules.rule: Place the edition tag last in the name, separated from the preceding text by a single ASCII space. For a file it goes after the rest of the base name and immediately before the extension: "Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4", and "Blade Runner (1982).1080p.hevc {edition-Director's Cut}.mkv", where version tokens are dot-separated but the edition tag is still space-separated. A folder takes the tag in the same final position: "/Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Director's Cut}". Folder tagging is not a substitute for file tagging: the page's only folder example repeats the tag on every file inside that folder. Confidence: the end-of-filename placement is stated in the page's prose; the single-space separator and the before-extension position are demonstrated by all seven of the page's examples but never stated as rules, and the page defers folder naming specifics to the separate "Naming and organizing your Movie files" article.

A movie file with no {edition-...} tag in its name is the ordinary, non-edition item for that movie (the page calls it "the original release", and elsewhere "a regular, non-edition movie" that still syncs watch state), and it can live in the same library alongside tagged editions of the same movie, each edition in its own folder. The tag on the filename is what marks an edition, so an untagged folder does not by itself signify the base release: tagged files inside an untagged folder are still that edition. When using the folder method, the page's example carries the tag on the edition folder and on every file inside it.
examples:
/Movies
   /Blade Runner (1982)
      Blade Runner (1982).mp4
   /Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Director's Cut}
      Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4

rules.rule: To combine editions with multi-version support, give each edition its own folder named with the edition tag (for example "/Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Director's Cut}/"), and give every version file inside that folder the same {edition-...} tag at the end of its filename, with the version descriptors (resolution, codec) placed before the tag, as in "Blade Runner (1982).1080p.h264 {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4". The untagged base release stays in its own separate untagged folder ("/Blade Runner (1982)/Blade Runner (1982).mp4"). Plex directs you to set the edition through file naming and not just by editing the movie information in the web app. Use a plain ASCII apostrophe inside the braces. Specifying editions at all requires a Plex Pass subscription on the server admin account.
examples:
/Media
   /Movies
      /Blade Runner (1982)
         Blade Runner (1982).mp4
      /Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Director's Cut}
         Blade Runner (1982).1080p.h264 {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4
         Blade Runner (1982).1080p.hevc {edition-Director's Cut}.mkv
         Blade Runner (1982).4k.h264 {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4
         Blade Runner (1982).4k.hevc {edition-Director's Cut}.mkv

rules.rule: Specifying edition information requires a Plex Pass subscription on the Plex Media Server admin account: "The ability to specify different editions for a movie requires a Plex Pass subscription for Server admin account." If the subscription expires, nothing happens to the existing library, but you can no longer add edition information to new content, nor change the information on any existing Editions. Caveat to carry with the rule: the same page also says "Anyone running a Plex Media Server can specify an edition for a movie simply by naming the video file correctly", and it never states what a {edition-...} filename tag does on a server with no Plex Pass. Do not claim the tag is silently ignored for non-subscribers; the page does not say so and partly contradicts it.
examples: No Plex Pass: {edition-Director's Cut} in a filename will not create an edition
Expired Plex Pass: existing editions keep working, but cannot be edited

rules.rule: Editions are a movie-only feature: Plex documents no support for Editions of TV Shows or Episodes ("There is not support for  Editions of TV Shows or Episodes at this time"). Never emit an {edition-...} tag in a filename or folder name for TV content (shows, seasons, or episodes); emit it only for movie files, in the form Title (Year) {edition-Name}.ext. Note this restricts editions only: Plex's separate multi-VERSION support (same content at different resolutions or encodings) does apply to episodes as well as movies, so do not extend this prohibition to version stacking. The page does not state how Plex handles an edition tag found on an episode file, so treat this as a do-not-emit rule rather than an assumption that Plex will strip or reject it.

Editions are a movies-only feature and require a Plex Pass subscription on the server admin account. Each edition of a movie is a separate library item: all editions of a movie are displayed as separate entries in the library grid, and their watched status, user ratings and metadata (including poster) are tracked per item, which is why Plex advises editing each item to give it a distinguishing poster. An item with no {edition-...} tag counts as one edition (the original release) alongside its tagged siblings. The details page of an item that has edition information displays a tag with that edition name, and when two or more editions of the same movie are in the library, each of their details pages also gets an "Other Editions of [movie]" section linking the others. Caveat: items carrying edition information are excluded from watch state and ratings syncing, so "tracked separately" here also means not synced at all. Separate rule, but load-bearing for renaming: adding an edition by renaming an existing file creates a new library item on the next scan and drops its watched status and metadata edits, whereas adding the Edition tag via the web app's Edit page (4.87.1+) converts the existing item and carries them over.
examples: Blade Runner (1982) and Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Final Cut} appear as two grid entries
Details page shows the tag "Final Cut"

rules.rule: Adding an edition tag by renaming a file that is already in the library causes Plex to treat it as a new library item on the next scan; the previous item's watched status and metadata customizations do not carry over. Plex's own recommendation is to set the Edition instead from the item's Edit page in the Plex Web app, which converts the existing library item and carries watched status and metadata customizations over. The Edit method requires Plex Web app 4.87.1 or newer and a Plex Pass subscription on the Server admin account; file naming has no such version requirement, though specifying editions at all is a Plex Pass feature. Note separately that syncing of watch state and ratings does not currently work with movie editions.
examples: Rename Blade Runner (1982).mp4 -> Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Final Cut}.mp4 : watched state lost
Edit > Edition field in Plex Web: watched state preserved

rules.rule: As an alternative to file naming, the edition of an existing library item can be set from the Edit page in the Plex Web app, version 4.87.1 or newer: adding or editing the Edition tag there converts the existing item to that edition and carries over its watched status and metadata customizations, unlike renaming the file, which the page warns creates a new library item on the next scan and loses both. Requires a Plex Pass subscription on the Server admin account (an expired Plex Pass blocks adding or changing editions, though existing ones are kept). This method does not cover every case: to have multiple versions (resolutions or encodings) within a single edition, Plex says to use the file naming method rather than editing in the web app.
examples: Plex Web 4.87.1+ > Edit movie > Edition field

rules.rule: Plex's "Sync Watch State and Ratings" feature currently excludes any movie carrying edition information. Even with syncing enabled on the account, a regular non-edition movie syncs its watch state and rating, but an item that has an edition set is not included in syncing. Edition information counts whether it came from the {edition-Name} filename token or from the Edit page in Plex Web 4.87.1 or newer. Editions apply to movies only; TV shows and episodes have no edition support, so this exclusion cannot arise for them. Related caveat when renaming: adding an edition token to an existing file makes Plex treat it as a new library item on the next scan, discarding the prior watched status and metadata customization.
examples: Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Final Cut}.mkv -> does not sync

rules.rule: Keep each major content type in its own dedicated folder tree. The folder you register as a Movie library's content location must contain movie content only, with no TV, music, or other content type under that same path. That folder does not have to sit at the filesystem root: in Plex's own example it is /Media/Movies, alongside /Media/TV Shows and /Media/Music. It is the main folder of each content type (e.g. /Movies, /Music, /TV Shows) that you specify as the content location for that library type. Plex states its scanners and metadata agents "will only work correctly" when the major content types are separated; mixing movie and television content under one path can cause incorrect matching, poorly classified content, and some files being ignored entirely.

A movie file's base name begins with the movie name, then a single space, then the release year wrapped in round parentheses, and ends with the file extension: `MovieName (release year).ext` (page examples: `Avatar (2009).mkv`, `Batman Begins (2005).mp4`, `Top Gun (1986).mkv`, `Blade Runner (1982).mp4`). That `MovieName (release year)` prefix is required; it is not necessarily the entire base name. The same page documents optional elements that may follow the year, each separated by a space, before the extension: an edition tag in curly braces of the form `{edition-[Edition Name]}` (`Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4`), an agent id in curly braces of the form `{imdb-tt0372784}` or `{tmdb-272}` (`Batman Begins (2005) {imdb-tt0372784}.mp4`), and, for a single movie split across several files, a split suffix written as ` - pt1` / ` - cd1` (`The Dark Knight (2008) - pt1.mp4`). The recommended layout puts that same string on the enclosing folder: `/Movies/MovieName (release year)/MovieName (release year).ext`. Note also that the page never states in words whether the year is mandatory, and it says nothing about resolution or release-group text, so neither can be cited from this source.

Year format: the release year is written in round parentheses immediately after the title, separated from it by exactly one space, as shown in the page's own patterns "MovieName (release year).ext" and "/Movies/MovieName (release year)/MovieName (release year).ext". Every year the article prints is four digits (2009, 2005, 1982, 1986, 2008), so four digits is the safe form to emit, though the page itself only says "release year" and never states a digit count, nor whether the year is optional. The same "Title (year)" string is used for the per-movie folder name as well as the filename. The year sits between the title and everything that follows it: any {imdb-...} / {tmdb-...} match tag, any {edition-...} tag, and any split-part suffix ("Title (year) - pt1.ext") all come after the closing parenthesis. The article shows no other year form: no square brackets, no curly braces around a year, no dot or underscore separators, and no zero-padded or non-four-digit years.

Put each movie in its own folder, named the same as the movie file: /Movies/MovieName (release year)/MovieName (release year).ext. Plex calls this the recommended method because it can sometimes significantly increase the speed of scanning in new media, and because it is where external media for a movie belongs (custom poster, external subtitle files, extras). Movie files placed next to each other directly in a main folder are also supported and must not be treated as an error, but Plex still recommends individual folders. The page stops short of "required" for local assets: it says the structure is not particularly important unless you have local media assets like posters or subtitles for a particular movie, in which case you should keep the movie and its assets together in an individual folder.

Per-movie folders are Plex's recommended layout, not a hard requirement. The page states movie files "can be placed into individual folders and this is the recommended method", and separately supports a flat layout: "If you wish, you can also put movie files next to each other in a main folder", e.g. /Movies/Avatar (2009).mkv. When a per-movie folder IS used, the folder name should equal the movie file's base name, giving /Movies/MovieName (release year)/MovieName (release year).ext, e.g. /Movies/Avatar (2009)/Avatar (2009).mkv and /Movies/Batman Begins (2005)/Batman Begins (2005).mp4. Optional curly-brace tags carry through to both names identically: /Movies/Batman Begins (2005) {imdb-tt0372784}/Batman Begins (2005) {imdb-tt0372784}.mp4, and /Movies/Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Final Cut}/Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Final Cut}.mkv. Two documented departures from exact equality: split or multi-part movies must sit in a folder named as usual for the movie while each file appends a part suffix (cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX or ptX), e.g. /Movies/The Dark Knight (2008)/The Dark Knight (2008) - pt1.mp4 and ... - pt2.mp4; and non-movie sidecars inside the folder follow their own conventions and are out of scope for this rule, e.g. Batman Begins (2005).en.srt and poster.jpg.

Movie files may be placed flat, side by side, directly in the library's main folder (e.g. /Movies) rather than in per-movie folders. Plex documents this layout as supported, provided each file is named "MovieName (release year).ext", but still recommends individual per-movie folders, which also speed up scanning of new media. Structure is not otherwise important for a plain single-file movie, and flat layout even supports multiple editions via the "{edition-Name}" filename tag. Per-movie folders become required once the movie has local media assets (poster, external subtitles, extras), when the movie is split across multiple part files (those must sit in their own folder), and when multiple editions are combined with local trailers or extras. Examples: /Movies/Avatar (2009).mkv, /Movies/Batman Begins (2005).mp4

Wherever `.ext` appears in the documented patterns (the movie file pattern `/Movies/MovieName (release year)/MovieName (release year).ext` and the split/stacked pattern `/Movies/MovieName (release year)/MovieName (release year) - Split_Name.ext`), it is a placeholder: write the file's actual video container extension, for example `.mkv` or `.mp4`, as in `Avatar (2009).mkv` and `Batman Begins (2005).mp4`. Sidecar files are documented with their real extension already, not with `.ext` (for example `Batman Begins (2005).en.srt`), so do not substitute a container extension there. Beware that some operating systems, Windows in particular, hide file extensions by default, so verify the true extension before renaming.

Optionally include an IMDb or TheMovieDB id in curly braces to help Plex match the movie, in the form {[source]-[id]}: source token `imdb` with the full IMDb id including its `tt` prefix (for example {imdb-tt0372784}), or source token `tmdb` with the bare numeric id (for example {tmdb-272}). Only these two source tokens are documented for movies. The page requires the library to use the current "Plex Movie" metadata agent, and states no minimum Plex Media Server version for this feature (the v1.28.1 and non-"legacy" agent floor on the same page applies to the separate {edition-[Edition Name]} tag, not to external IDs). The documented examples place the tag after the year and repeat it on both the movie folder and the filename, but the page states no positional requirement, so treat "after the year, on folder and filename" as the documented convention rather than a mandate.

Encode a movie edition in curly braces as {edition-[Edition Name]}, where Edition Name is free text ("whatever normal text you want") of at most 32 characters. Placement depends on library layout: in a flat/grouped library (all movie files directly under /Movies, no per-movie folder) the tag must be part of the filename, e.g. "Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4"; when using the recommended one-folder-per-movie layout you may put it on the folder name, the filename, or both, and Plex recommends both for consistency, e.g. "/Movies/Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Director's Cut}/Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4". The tag may be combined with a {[source]-[id]} tag and the order of the tags does not matter. Prerequisites: the feature requires a Plex Pass subscription on the Plex Media Server admin account, and works only with the non-legacy Plex Movie agent on Plex Media Server v1.28.1 or newer; without both, the edition tag has no effect. Related note: if you supply local trailers or extras alongside multiple editions, use individual folders per edition and place the extras in the edition you treat as the main one (or copy them into each).

Edition tags of the form {edition-[Edition Name]} are only available when using the non-legacy Plex Movie agent on Plex Media Server v1.28.1 and newer, and specifying different editions for a movie additionally requires a Plex Pass subscription on the Plex Media Server admin account. The page does not say how the tag is treated when either condition is unmet.
examples: Plex Media Server v1.28.1 and newer, non-legacy "Plex Movie" agent

rules.rule: Edition tags use the form {edition-[Edition Name]} (any normal text, max 32 characters) and require a Plex Pass subscription on the Plex Media Server admin account plus the non-legacy Plex Movie agent on Plex Media Server v1.28.1 or newer. When using individual folders per movie, the edition tag may be placed in the folder name, the file name, or both; Plex recommends both for consistency, so prefer that. Each edition gets its own sibling folder, and the un-editioned base file lives in its own plain folder alongside them, for example /Movies/Blade Runner (1982)/Blade Runner (1982).mp4, /Movies/Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Director's Cut}/Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4, /Movies/Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Final Cut}/Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Final Cut}.mkv. The edition tag can be combined with a {[source]-[id]} tag, and tag order does not matter. If local trailers or extras are also provided for a movie with multiple editions, per-edition folders are required, with the extras placed in the chosen main edition (or copied alongside each edition).

Both brace tags may appear on the same movie folder name or filename, and their relative order is not significant: \"Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Final Cut} {imdb-tt0083658}.mkv\" and \"Blade Runner (1982) {imdb-tt0083658} {edition-Final Cut}.mkv\" are equally valid. Both tags follow the \"Title (release year)\" portion of the name. A parser must accept either ordering; a renamer should not reorder existing tags to satisfy a canonical form, since neither order is more correct. Caveats the source attaches: the page states this rule but never illustrates it (every on-page example carries only one kind of tag, so the combined examples above are constructed, not quoted); the guidance appears in the individual-folders-per-movie section, where the edition tag may go on the folder name, the filename, or both, with both recommended for consistency; {edition-[Edition Name]} requires a Plex Pass, the non-legacy Plex Movie agent, and Plex Media Server v1.28.1 or newer, with a 32-character limit on the edition name; {[source]-[id]} requires the current \"Plex Movie\" metadata agent and takes an imdb or tmdb id.

A movie split across multiple files must live in its own folder named exactly as a normal movie folder, "MovieName (release year)", and each part file is named "MovieName (release year) <sep> Split_Name.ext". Split_Name must be one of a closed set: cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX, ptX, where X is the part number (cd1, cd2, ...). The separator is ambiguous in the source: the template line prints an en dash ("MovieName (release year) – Split_Name.ext") while the worked example uses a space-hyphen-space ("The Dark Knight (2008) - pt1.mp4"); prefer the example's " - " when generating names and accept either when parsing. Additional constraints from the same section: at most 8 parts per stack, all parts in the same container format (all MP4 or all MKV), identical audio and subtitle streams in the same order across parts, and no stacking support in "Other Videos" libraries or libraries using the Plex Video Files Scanner. Plex labels stacking as limited support and recommends joining the parts into one file instead.

The part token (Split_Name) is one of exactly six forms listed by the page: cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX, ptX, where X is replaced by the part number. The page prints all six lowercase and gives no uppercase or mixed-case variant, so emit lowercase as the canonical form, but note the article states no case requirement, so do not treat a differently-cased token as a documented violation. No zero-padded form (cd01, part01) appears and the page is silent on padding, so emit unpadded numbers and treat padded input as undocumented rather than as invalid. The part number is bounded by the same section's statement that "Only stacks up to 8 parts are supported". Examples actually printed on the page: cd1, cd2 (in the parenthetical) and pt1, pt2 (in the Dark Knight file listing); the other four token families appear only as the abstract X forms.

In a movie library, a stack may contain at most 8 parts. Stacks of 9 or more parts are not supported (the page does not specify what happens beyond 8, only that it is unsupported, so do not assert a specific failure mode). Parts are the files sharing one movie folder and base name, distinguished by a cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX, or ptX suffix; pt1 through pt8 is a valid maximum-size stack. This allowance does not extend to "Other Videos" libraries or libraries using the "Plex Video Files Scanner", which do not support stacked content at all.
examples: pt1 through pt8 is the maximum

rules.rule: Within a stacked (split) movie, every part must use the same file format, for example all MP4 or all MKV; mixing formats across parts of one stack is unsupported. Scope: files named MovieName (year) - cdX/discX/diskX/dvdX/partX/ptX inside that movie's own folder. Related constraints from the same section: all parts should have identical audio and subtitle streams in the same order, and only stacks of up to 8 parts are supported.
examples: The Dark Knight (2008) - pt1.mp4 + The Dark Knight (2008) - pt2.mp4

rules.rule: All parts of a stacked (split) movie should have identical audio and subtitle streams, in the same order. This appears as a "should" in the Notes for split movies on the movie-naming page, alongside the harder constraint that all parts must be the same file format (e.g. all MP4 or all MKV) and a maximum of 8 parts. The page also warns that audio/subtitle stream selection across parts is one of the features that may not work correctly with split files, and recommends joining the parts into a single file instead of stacking.
examples: all parts: track1 EN AC3, track2 DE AC3, sub1 EN

rules.rule: Stacked (split) content is not supported in "Other Videos" libraries, nor in any library using the "Plex Video Files Scanner". Verbatim: “Other Videos” libraries or those using the “Plex Video Files Scanner” do not support stacked content. Playback support is also not universal across clients: "Not all Plex apps support playback of stacked media", and the page notes split files play as a single item "in most, but not all, players". Implementation note: the constraint is on the library type and the scanner, not on the metadata agent. The page does not say to use the "Plex Movie" agent for stacks, so the requirement is that the file live in a Movies library that is not using the Plex Video Files Scanner. The page additionally warns that stacking is not the expected way to handle content and "may negatively impact usage of various Plex features (including, but not limited to, preview thumbnails, chapter images, audio/subtitle stream selection across parts, and more)", recommending users join the parts into a single file instead.
examples: Use a Movies library with the Plex Movie agent for stacked files
Not all Plex apps support playback of stacked media

rules.rule: Prefer joining split parts into one video file rather than relying on stacking. Plex supports stacked content only in a limited way and warns it "may negatively impact usage of various Plex features (including, but not limited to, preview thumbnails, chapter images, audio/subtitle stream selection across parts, and more)"; the list is explicitly non-exhaustive. Plex "strongly encourage[s]" using a tool to join or merge the parts into a single video. Stacking additionally carries hard limits: max 8 parts, all parts in the same container format, identical audio and subtitle streams in the same order, playback unsupported in some Plex apps, and no stacking support at all in "Other Videos" libraries or libraries using the "Plex Video Files Scanner". If you do stack, put the parts in the movie's own folder and name them "MovieName (release year) - Split_Name.ext" where Split_Name is cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX or ptX, for example "The Dark Knight (2008) - pt1.mp4" and "The Dark Knight (2008) - pt2.mp4". Example of the preferred approach: merge "The Dark Knight (2008) - pt1.mkv" and "- pt2.mkv" into a single "The Dark Knight (2008).mkv". Plex names no official merging tool; it links an unofficial community forum guide that uses MKVToolNix GUI, so treat that tool as a community suggestion rather than a Plex recommendation.
examples: Merge pt1.mkv + pt2.mkv into The Dark Knight (2008).mkv with MKVToolNix

rules.rule: When a movie has multiple editions AND you supply your own local trailers or extras files, Plex recommends giving each edition its own folder (each named with its own {edition-Name} tag, sitting directly under the movie library root, as in "/Movies/Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Final Cut}/") and placing the local extras in whichever edition you choose to treat as the "main" one. Copying the extras alongside every edition is an explicitly sanctioned alternative, not a fallback. Note that the folder-per-edition requirement applies to this extras case; without local extras, the page also permits edition-tagged files sitting flat in the library or in a single movie folder. The article does not itself document the extras subfolder names (Trailers, Featurettes, Deleted Scenes and so on); those come from Plex's separate local media assets article, so do not cite this page for them.
examples: copy the same extras into each edition folder

rules.rule: When a movie has local assets (custom poster or background images, external subtitle files, extras), keep the movie file and those assets together in that movie's own folder, for example /Movies/Batman Begins (2005)/ holding Batman Begins (2005).mp4, Batman Begins (2005).en.srt and poster.jpg. Individual folders are the recommended layout in general; stand-alone files placed directly in the library root are supported but not recommended, and the page makes co-location explicit for the local-assets case: "in which you should have the movie and assets together in an individual folder". For Plex to use these files they must be named and organized as documented and the Local Media Assets source must be enabled and ordered correctly; this page does not say where that setting is configured, it links to the separate "Local Media Assets - Movies" article.

The part marker (Plex calls it Split_Name) is the trailing token of a multi-part movie filename, following the "MovieName (release year)" portion after a space-dash-space separator, as in "The Dark Knight (2008) - pt1.mp4". It must be one of exactly six keyword stems: cd, disc, disk, dvd, part, pt. The page writes these as cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX, ptX and instructs "replace `X` with the appropriate number (cd1, cd2, etc.)", so X is the part number written directly after the stem with no intervening separator. The page lists no other multi-part form. It says nothing about case sensitivity, so treat case handling as unspecified by this rule rather than as permitted or forbidden.

Replace the literal X in the keyword (cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX, ptX) with the part's number written as a plain, unpadded integer. The page's exact instruction is to use "the appropriate number (cd1, cd2, etc.)"; it never states a starting value or a padding width. Every example it shows (cd1, cd2, pt1, pt2) is a single unpadded digit beginning at 1, so treat "start at 1, no zero-padding" as inferred from the examples rather than as a stated requirement. The page separately caps a stack with "Only stacks up to 8 parts are supported", so the substituted number is in practice 1 through 8.

Append the part marker at the very end of the otherwise-normal movie filename, after the movie name, the parenthesised release year, and any {edition-...} or {source-id} tags, separated by space + ASCII hyphen-minus (U+002D) + space, and immediately followed by the file extension: "MovieName (release year) - Split_Name.ext". Split_Name is one of cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX, ptX, with X replaced by the part number (cd1, cd2, ...). Note that the page's abstract template renders the separator as an en dash (U+2013), but its two concrete examples ("The Dark Knight (2008) - pt1.mp4", "The Dark Knight (2008) - pt2.mp4") use a plain hyphen; treat the en dash as a typographic artifact and emit the hyphen. This rule governs the filename only: the same page separately requires that all parts of a split movie be placed inside their own folder named "MovieName (release year)".

In the "Movies Split Across Multiple Files" section only, the abstract pattern "/Movies/MovieName (release year)/MovieName (release year) – Split_Name.ext" prints the separator as an en dash (U+2013), while the worked example directly below it prints "The Dark Knight (2008) - pt1.mp4" with an ASCII hyphen-minus (U+002D). The en dash is typographic styling introduced by the CMS in prose markup (code blocks on the page are exempt and consistently use the hyphen), not a literal requirement. When writing filenames, emit the ASCII hyphen form " - " as shown in the example; when parsing existing filenames, accept both U+002D and U+2013. Note also that the page identifies only the Split_Name token (cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX, ptX, X replaced by a number, up to 8 parts) as the significant element, and states no requirement about the separator character at all. No other naming pattern on the page uses a separator, so this applies to split or stacked media only.

In a Movies library using a movie scanner/agent, every part of a split (stacked) movie must live inside a folder for that movie, and that folder is named with the normal movie naming (MovieName (release year)), carrying no part marker; the part marker appears only on the filenames inside it, as MovieName (release year) - Split_Name.ext where Split_Name is cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX or ptX. Example: /Movies/The Dark Knight (2008)/The Dark Knight (2008) - pt1.mp4 and .../The Dark Knight (2008) - pt2.mp4. Stacking is not supported in Other Videos libraries or with the "Plex Video Files Scanner".

Every part of a split movie follows the same documented pattern, "MovieName (release year) - Split_Name.ext", inside a folder named "MovieName (release year)". Consequently all parts in a stack share a byte-identical base name (title, year in parentheses, and any {imdb-...}, {tmdb-...} or {edition-...} tags) and the same file extension, differing only in the number inside the trailing split marker, which must be one of cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX or ptX. Detect the marker by keyword, not by the separator character: the article's format line renders the separator as an en dash while its own example uses a space-hyphen-space. A stack holds at most 8 parts.
examples: The Dark Knight (2008) - pt1.mp4 and The Dark Knight (2008) - pt2.mp4 (valid pair)
The Dark Knight (2008) - pt1.mp4 and The Dark Knight - pt2.mp4 (invalid: base names differ)

rules.rule: A movie stack may contain at most 8 parts: "Only stacks up to 8 parts are supported". Apply the limit to the number of files grouped into one stack (the members), not to the numeric value in the split suffix. When a detected stack has 9 or more members, warn that Plex supports only up to 8 parts; do not treat the individual filename as invalid, since this is a stated support limitation rather than a naming-syntax rule. A high part number on its own (for example cd9) is only a violation when it makes the stack exceed 8 members; the page states no upper bound on the index itself. The limit applies to the split forms cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX and ptX, with all parts in the movie's own folder. Related limits from the same Notes list, worth surfacing separately: all parts must share one file format, and "Other Videos" libraries or those using the "Plex Video Files Scanner" do not support stacked content at all.
examples: cd1 through cd8 is the maximum valid range
cd9 exceeds the supported stack size

rules.rule: Within a single stack (the split parts of one movie, placed in their own movie-named folder and differing only in the trailing cdX / discX / diskX / dvdX / partX / ptX token), every part must be the same file format. Source wording: "All parts must be of the same file format (e.g. all MP4 or all MKV)". Implement it as: group the files Plex would stack, then flag the stack if its parts do not all share one container. Comparing file extensions is the practical proxy and correctly rejects cases like "Movie (2008) - pt1.mkv" plus "Movie (2008) - pt2.mp4". Be aware the page constrains format, not extension, so extensions that denote the same container (.mp4 with .m4v) satisfy the letter of the rule even if a strict extension-equality check flags them.

Applies only to movies split across multiple files (stacked parts named cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX or ptX, placed inside the movie's own folder). Across those parts, the audio and subtitle streams should be identical and in the same order. Plex states this with "should", unlike the adjacent "All parts must be of the same file format", so it is advisory rather than a scanner-enforced requirement. It is not cosmetic: the same section warns that split files can degrade "audio/subtitle stream selection across parts", which is the behaviour this bullet protects. A renamer cannot check this from filenames; it needs container inspection (ffprobe or mediainfo) comparing the ordered audio and subtitle track lists of every part in the stack, and should surface a mismatch as a warning, never as a rename blocker.
examples: Each part muxed with the same track order: [eng AC3, ger AC3, eng SRT]

rules.rule: Stacked (split) naming is only honored in libraries whose scanner supports it. Per the source, "“Other Videos” libraries or those using the “Plex Video Files Scanner” do not support stacked content." Check the library's type and its configured scanner, not its metadata agent: a Movie library set to the Plex Video Files Scanner is still excluded, and the Plex Movie agent is irrelevant to stacking (the page invokes it only for {imdb-}/{tmdb-} ID matching and {edition-} naming). In an excluded library, cd1/disc1/pt1-style parts are not combined into one playable item and each file is listed separately, so do not rely on stacked naming there. Corrected examples: "Movie library using a scanner other than the Plex Video Files Scanner: stacking supported"; "Movie library configured with the Plex Video Files Scanner: stacking not supported"; "Other Videos library: stacking not supported". Note this sits alongside the section's other stacking limits: all parts in one folder named for the movie, identical file format across parts, identical audio and subtitle streams in the same order, at most 8 parts, and not all Plex apps can play stacked media.
examples: Movie library with the Plex Movie agent: stacking supported
Other Videos library: stacking not supported

rules.rule: Plex supports split (stacked) files only in a limited way and calls it "not the expected way to handle content". Where the parts can be merged, prefer joining them into a single video file: the page strongly encourages using a tool to join/merge, because splitting "may negatively impact" preview thumbnails, chapter images, audio/subtitle stream selection across parts, and other features. Do not treat this as a prohibition. Stacks remain supported and must still be recognised: name them MovieName (release year) - <keyword><n>.ext inside /Movies/MovieName (release year)/, using one of cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX, ptX (for example The Dark Knight (2008) - pt1.mp4 and The Dark Knight (2008) - pt2.mp4), with at most 8 parts, every part in the same file format, and identical audio/subtitle streams in the same order across parts. Stacking is not available in "Other Videos" libraries and not every Plex app can play stacked content. The page names no particular merging tool, so any tool suggestion (MKVToolNix, ffmpeg) is the implementer's own choice, not a Plex recommendation.
examples: Merge Movie (2008) - pt1.mkv and pt2.mkv into Movie (2008).mkv with MKVToolNix

rules.rule: Treat stacked (split) playback as best-effort, never guaranteed. Plex states that split files "can be played back as a single item (in most, but not all, players)", that "Not all Plex apps support playback of stacked media", and that "Not all features will work correctly when using 'split' files"; the page specifically calls out preview thumbnails, chapter images, and audio/subtitle stream selection across parts as likely to degrade. Two limits are absolute rather than best-effort: "Other Videos" libraries and libraries using the "Plex Video Files Scanner" do not support stacked content at all, and only stacks up to 8 parts are supported. Because Plex "strongly encourage[s] you to instead use a tool to join/merge the individual files into a single video", a renamer should emit a warning whenever it produces stacked names and point the user at joining, rather than treating a stack as a normal successful outcome. Do not name specific clients: the source never identifies which players or apps do or do not support stacking, so any app-level example is unsourced speculation.
examples: A stacked movie may play on Plex Web but fail to play as one item on some TV apps

rules.rule: The base name preceding a part marker is the standard movie base name "MovieName (release year)", where release year is the four-digit year in round parentheses (every example on the page uses four digits, e.g. Avatar (2009), Batman Begins (2005), The Dark Knight (2008)). The base name may optionally carry a trailing identifier in curly braces, " {imdb-ttNNNNNNN}" or " {tmdb-NNN}", and when present that suffix is part of the base name. The containing folder is named with the identical base name string, suffix included: "/Movies/MovieName (release year)/MovieName (release year).ext" for a single file, and "/Movies/MovieName (release year)/MovieName (release year) - Split_Name.ext" for a stacked one, where Split_Name is one of cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX, ptX. The page's only worked stacked example is "/Movies/The Dark Knight (2008)/The Dark Knight (2008) - pt1.mp4" and "- pt2.mp4"; the Avatar cd1 and Batman Begins cd2 examples are derived from the documented patterns, not quoted from the page.

With the current (non-legacy) "Plex Movie" agent, a movie file or folder name may carry optional tags in curly braces after the "Name (year)" part. The matching tag must follow the form {[source]-[id]}, where source is imdb or tmdb as shown in the page's examples (Batman Begins (2005) {imdb-tt0372784}.mp4, Batman Begins (2005) {tmdb-272}.mp4). The edition tag must follow the form {edition-[Edition Name]}, where the name is any normal text up to 32 characters (Blade Runner (1982) {edition-Director's Cut}.mp4); editions additionally require a Plex Pass subscription on the server admin account and the non-legacy Plex Movie agent on Plex Media Server v1.28.1 or newer. Either tag may appear on the movie folder name, the filename, or both, and Plex recommends putting edition information in both. The two tags can be combined, and the order of the tags is not important.

When organizing home media as a series (Show / Season-by-year folders, filenames of the form ShowName - s{YEAR}e{NN} - Description.ext, matched by the "Personal Media Shows" agent), the library must be created with the TV Shows library type, not the Home Videos library type. The library's display title is unconstrained and may still be "Home Videos". This applies to that series layout only; the Home Videos library type remains valid for home media not organized as a series.
examples: Library type: TV Shows; Library title: "Home Videos" (allowed)
Library type: Home Videos (NOT allowed for this layout)

rules.rule: Create the library as a TV/Shows library, not a Home Videos library (the page: "you must make a “TV” Library, not a “Home Videos” Library, though you can still call it Home Videos if you like"), and use the TV "Personal Media Shows" agent for it. That agent, combined with TV-series-style filenames, presents the videos in three levels, Show > Season > Episodes: /Home Movies/Christmas/2012/Christmas - s2012e01 - Getting Ready.m4v yields Show "Christmas", Season 2012, Episodes 1..n. The agent does not do this on its own; the sYYYYeNN filename pattern is what supplies the season and episode. Caveat from the page: episodes display only as "Episode 1", "Episode 2" and any title text in the filename is ignored. The article documents no explicit step for assigning the agent; the one Settings path it gives is Settings > [your Plex Media Server] > Agents > [Library Type] > [Agent], and it is given there to confirm Local Media Assets is checked and topmost so embedded metadata in MP4/M4V/MOV files is used.
examples: Settings > Server > Agents > Shows > Personal Media Shows

rules.rule: In a Plex "TV" library using the "Personal Media Shows" agent (the page states you must create a "TV" library, not a "Home Videos" library, though you may still name it Home Videos), lay the files out in the three presentation levels the page shows: library root / <ShowFolder> / <SeasonFolder> / <video file>. The show folder supplies the "show" name (Christmas in the example), the folder inside it supplies the season (2012), and the video files sit directly in that season folder. The page shows no other layout: it gives no example of files at the show-folder level and no example of a deeper nesting, so treat the show folder and season folder as both required. In the page's example the season folder is a year whose value matches the sYYYY token in the filenames (/2012 holds s2012e01 and up, /2013 holds s2013e01), though the page does not state that the folder name and the season token must agree as a separate requirement.

Name each file "<ShowName> - s<Season>e<Episode> - <Title>.<ext>", with the ASCII hyphen-minus U+002D surrounded by exactly one U+0020 space on each side (" - ") as the separator between the three components, in that order. The season/episode token is lowercase "s" and lowercase "e" with nothing between the two parts. For home series media the season is the 4-digit calendar year and the episode is zero-padded to 2 digits (s2012e01), matching the enclosing year folder in the layout the page shows: /Home Movies/<ShowName>/<Year>/. The <Title> component appears in every example on the page but the page notes it is currently ignored by Plex, which shows episodes only as "Episode 1", "Episode 2" and so on, so treat it as optional descriptive text rather than a parsed field. Note that the page states no template in prose; this pattern is inferred from its four code-block examples (Christmas - s2012e01 - Getting Ready.m4v and siblings), and it applies to a library created as a "TV" library using the "Personal Media Shows" agent, not a "Home Videos" library.

Write the season/episode token as a lowercase "s" immediately followed by the season digits, then a lowercase "e" immediately followed by the episode digits, with no space, dot, or other character anywhere inside the token. Every example on the page uses this form: s2012e01, s2012e02, s2012e03, s2013e01. In this page's context the "season" is the four-digit year of the home-video event, matching the parent folder (2012, 2013), and the episode number is zero-padded to two digits. The token sits between space-hyphen-space separators, as in "Christmas - s2012e01 - Getting Ready.m4v". Note that the page establishes this format by example only: it makes no statement about whether letter case matters, and it never mentions S2012E01, s2012 e01 or 2012x01. Treat those as unattested on this page rather than as forms this page rejects; if a naming tool needs to reject them, that decision has to be sourced elsewhere.

In the Home Series layout (library root > show folder > year folder > episode files), each filename begins with the name of the show folder, which is the file's grandparent directory and not its immediate parent (the immediate parent is the year folder that supplies the season). That prefix is followed by " - " and then the sYYYYeXX token, as in show folder /Christmas containing /2012 containing "Christmas - s2012e01 - Getting Ready.m4v". The article shows this pattern in its single example rather than stating it as an explicit requirement, and Plex presents the show folder's name as the show title while ignoring any title text after the episode token.

In the article's example the season folder's name is repeated verbatim as the digits after the "s" in every file inside it: the folder 2012 holds s2012e01, s2012e02 and s2012e03, and the folder 2013 holds s2013e01. Note this is shown by example only, the page states no explicit matching rule, and the season folder does not have to be a year: the article describes the middle level generically as the "Season" level (TV Shows > Season > Episodes, e.g. Year > Event > Home Videos). The example also shows the season number is used unpadded and can exceed two digits, and the season folder sits inside the "show" folder whose name is repeated as the filename prefix (/Home Movies/Christmas/2012/Christmas - s2012e01 - ....m4v).

For home/personal media organized as a series (a "TV" library, not a "Home Videos" library, using the TV "Personal Media Shows" agent), a four-digit year is a valid season: name the folder with the bare year and use the same year as the season token in each filename, as ShowName - sYYYYeNN - Title.ext. The article's only worked example is /Home Movies/Christmas/2012/Christmas - s2012e01 - Getting Ready.m4v (plus /2013/Christmas - s2013e01), presented as "Show" Name: Christmas, Series: 2012, Episodes: Episode 1, Episode 2, Episode 3. The event is the show and the year is the season. The season comes from the sYYYY token in the filename, so a year-named folder alone is not sufficient. The article also warns that episode titles in the filename ("Getting Ready") are ignored and episodes display only as "Episode 1" etc. Do not apply this pattern to regular matched TV series libraries.

Zero-pad the episode number to at least two digits (e01, e02, e03). Every filename example on the Naming Home Series Media page uses two-digit episode tokens (s2012e01, s2012e02, s2012e03, s2013e01), but the page states this only by example and never documents a padding requirement in prose, so emit two-digit padding as the house convention rather than enforcing it as a parser constraint. Scope: only episodes 1 to 3 appear, so the page gives no guidance for episode 10 or higher; do not read "two digits" as a maximum width. The season token in these examples is a four-digit year (s2012) and must not be padded to two digits.

For home series handled by the TV "Personal Media Shows" agent (a TV-type library, not a Home Videos library), the trailing title component after the second " - " in "Show Name - sYYYYeXX - Episode Description.ext" is currently ignored for matching: the page says episodes are presented only as "Episode 1", "Episode 2", "Episode 3". Treat that component as cosmetic and never as a source of episode titles for this agent. Two caveats: the page scopes this to home-series media and says nothing about the standard TV show agent, so do not generalise the rule to regular series; and the page's "Using Embedded Metadata" section notes that MP4/M4V/MOV files with embedded metadata can supply richer titles when the Local Media Assets source is enabled and ordered topmost, so "Episode N" is the filename-derived result, not an absolute ceiling.
examples: "Getting Ready" in Christmas - s2012e01 - Getting Ready.m4v is ignored
Displayed episode titles: Episode 1, Episode 2, Episode 3

rules.rule: In a TV library using the "Personal Media Shows" agent, lay out home series media as three levels under the library root, for example /Home Movies/Christmas/2012/Christmas - s2012e01 - Getting Ready.m4v. The show folder ("Christmas") supplies the "Show" name, the year subfolder together with the matching sYYYY token in each filename supplies what Plex labels the "Series" (the season, "2012"), and each file becomes one episode. Expect episodes to be titled only "Episode 1", "Episode 2", "Episode 3" and so on: Plex ignores any additional descriptive text in the filename, such as "Getting Ready", so those titles will not appear.

Embedded (in-file) metadata is only usable if the video sits in a container that supports it, such as MP4, M4V, or MOV. The container alone is not enough: the Local Media Assets agent source must also be checked and placed topmost in the agent list (Settings > your server > Agents > pick the library type and agent). Embedded metadata supplements the naming convention rather than replacing it; files still need the Show - sYYYYeNN - Title.ext form, and the page notes that the trailing title text in the filename is currently ignored.

To have embedded metadata used, the Local Media Assets agent source must be both enabled and topmost in the source list. In the Plex Web App: Settings (top right of the Home screen) > select your Plex Media Server in the settings sidebar > Agents > choose the Library Type and Agent you want to change > ensure Local Media Assets is checked and ensure it is topmost in the list. For home series media the relevant combination is a TV library using the \"Personal Media Shows\" agent. Embedded metadata applies to filetypes that support it, e.g. MP4, M4V, MOV. The article specifies only that the source must end up topmost, not how to reorder it, so do not present drag-and-drop as documented behaviour.
examples: Settings > Agents > Shows > Personal Media Shows > [x] Local Media Assets, dragged to position 1

rules.rule: A file covering more than one consecutive episode of the same season carries exactly one episode token of the form s<SS>e<EE>-e<EE>: a lowercase "s", the two-digit season number, a lowercase "e", the two-digit number of the FIRST episode covered, an ASCII hyphen-minus (U+002D), a second lowercase "e", and the two-digit number of the LAST episode covered. Page template: "/TV Shows/ShowName/Season 02/ShowName - sXXeYY-eZZ - Optional_Info.ext"; page example: "s02e18-e19"; real listing example: "Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s02e01-e03.avi". The season marker appears only once in the token, so a range cannot span two seasons. Only the hyphen INSIDE the token is fixed; the separators between show name, token and optional info are free-form, because the page states "It does not matter if you use dashes, dots, or just spaces". Lowercase and two-digit zero padding are what every example on the page uses, though the page does not state them as an explicit requirement.

The episode-range token uses the documented format sXXeYY-eZZ, in which the two episode numbers are joined by a single ASCII hyphen-minus (U+002D). Both literal examples on the page, s02e18-e19 and s02e01-e03, contain no non-ASCII characters, and no alternative range form (eNN-NN, eNNeNN, or an en/em dash join) appears anywhere on the page. Note that the page states no explicit prohibition on other dash characters; the requirement is inferred from the documented format and from 2/2 examples. Note also that the page's flexibility clause ("It does not matter if you use dashes, dots, or just spaces") applies only to the separators between filename components (ShowName, the season/episode token, Optional_Info), not to the join inside the range token. Finally, the article's prose template displays the outer component separators as U+2013 en dashes through the CMS's smart-typography conversion; those are a rendering artifact, and the page's plain-text directory-tree example uses ASCII " - " for the same positions.

In a multi-episode filename, the second episode number carries its own lowercase "e" and the season marker is not repeated. The page's format line is "/TV Shows/ShowName/Season 02/ShowName – sXXeYY-eZZ – Optional_Info.ext", its stated example is "s02e18-e19", and its Examples tree corroborates with "Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s02e01-e03.avi". YY and ZZ are the first and last episode covered by the file (an inclusive range inside one season, which is why sXX appears once), joined by a literal hyphen with no surrounding spaces. Neither sXXeYY-ZZ nor sXXeYY-sXXeZZ appears anywhere on the page, so emit sXXeYY-eZZ; treat the others as unattested by the documentation rather than as forms the page declares invalid, since it never says so. Do not copy the en dashes from the format line: those surround Optional_Info as article typography, and the page states that the separator between the name, the notation and the optional info may be dashes, dots or spaces (its own Examples use " - "). Only the hyphen within the range itself is shown literally. All season and episode markers on the page are lowercase.

A single file covering more than one episode is named with a two-number range in the form sXXeYY-eZZ, where YY is the first and ZZ the last episode covered in the file (the "e" prefix repeats on the second number, the season does not; so s02e01-e03, not s02e01-03). Plex's page gives this as the only format for such files and gives no per-episode enumeration alternative, so a file holding three episodes is written first-to-last: Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s02e01-e03.avi. The page states only "the first and last episode covered in the file"; that the intervening episodes are covered is implied rather than stated, but it is confirmed by the page's own directory example, where s02e01-e03.avi is followed directly by s02e04.m4v with no separate files for e02 or e03, and by its note that "playing any of the represented episodes will play the full file". Note the page's caveat: multi-episode files appear as individual episodes in Plex apps but always play the whole file, and Plex recommends splitting the file into one file per episode instead.
examples: Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s02e01-e03.avi covers episodes 1, 2 and 3

rules.rule: Season and episode numbers are written zero-padded to at least two digits, both in the sXXeXX episode token and in the "Season NN" folder name. Every example on the page uses this form (s00e01, s00e13, s01e01, s01e02, s01e03, s02e01-e03, s02e04, s02e17, s02e18-e19, Season 00, Season 01, Season 02, Season 08), and the page states it outright for season zero: specials "are always part of season zero (i.e. season number \"00\")", and for miniseries: "you simply always use \"Season 01\" as the season". The page shows no season or episode number above 99, so treat two digits as a minimum width and never truncate a three-digit number to two. The page also does not say an unpadded form such as s2e17 is rejected; the only latitude it states is on separators ("It does not matter if you use dashes, dots, or just spaces"), so two-digit padding is the documented convention to write, not a documented requirement of the matcher.

The multi-episode file must sit at <LibraryRoot>/<ShowName>/<SeasonFolder>/<filename>, where <LibraryRoot> is the folder added as the library content location and directly contains one folder per show, and each show folder contains one folder per season. For regular seasons the folder is the literal English word "Season" followed by the season number, zero-padded to two digits in every documented example (Season 01, Season 02, Season 08); the English word "Season" is required even when the content is in another language ("Be sure to use the English word 'Season' when creating season directories, even if your content is in another language"). The single exception is season zero: specials go in a folder named either "Season 00" or "Specials", so a multi-episode specials file may legitimately sit in a folder whose name does not contain the word "Season".

When a season directory is used, it must be named with the English word "Season" followed by the season number, even if the content is in another language. Plex's own examples always capitalize "Season" and zero-pad to two digits (Season 01, Season 02, Season 08), though the page does not explicitly state that padding is mandatory. Season-zero content ("specials") is the only exception to the "Season" wording: it goes in a folder named either "Season 00" or "Specials". A miniseries always uses "Season 01".

Within the episode filename, components appear in this fixed order: ShowName, then a single middle token, then optional info, then the file extension. Only a separator may sit between ShowName and the middle token, and the page treats "dashes, dots, or just spaces" as equivalent separators (its templates print an en dash, U+2013, while all of its concrete examples use a plain hyphen). The middle token is whichever of these applies: `sXXeYY` for a season-based episode, `sXXeYY-eZZ` for one file covering an episode range (first and last episode), `s00eYY` for a special, or a date in `YYYY-MM-DD` or `DD-MM-YYYY` form (with dash, period, or space separators) for a date-based show. The ShowName component may itself include a parenthesised year, which the page recommends for the Plex TV Series agent; the year is part of the show name, not an intervening component. The trailing optional-info component is genuinely optional and may be omitted (`From the Earth to the Moon (1998) - s01e01.mp4`); it may be bracketed so matching ignores it (`[1080p Bluray]`); and for episodes split across files it is where the stack name goes (cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX, ptX). Source templates are full paths: the filename is always preceded by `/TV Shows/ShowName/Season NN/` (or `/Specials/` for season 00).

The characters separating the show name, the episode token and the optional info are not fixed. The article states "It does not matter if you use dashes, dots, or just spaces", so a parser must accept a hyphen, a dot or a space in those positions and must not require the en dash (U+2013) shown in the article's templates; the Examples section itself uses a plain ASCII hyphen (U+002D) throughout, for example "Doctor Who (1963) - s01e01 - An Unearthly Child (1).mp4". Two limits apply. First, the page names only these three separator styles, so treat anything else (an underscore, for instance) as unsupported: the article uses the underscore inside a field name, "Optional_Info", never as a separator. Second, the hyphen inside a multi-episode range such as "s02e18-e19" belongs to the episode token, not to the field separators, so it must be parsed as part of the sXXeYY-eZZ pattern rather than as a field boundary.

The trailing Optional_Info segment is optional. When present, legacy agents ignore it for matching, while the Plex TV Series agent uses it as a matching hint. Enclosing it in square brackets forces it to be ignored for matching in both cases, e.g. "Band of Brothers (2001) - s01e01 - Currahee [1080p Bluray].mkv". Square brackets are the mechanism here; parentheses are reserved for the year and are not a way to suppress optional info. A name may also carry no optional info at all, e.g. "Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s02e01-e03.avi".
examples: Band of Brothers (2001) - s01e01 - Currahee [1080p Bluray].mkv
Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s02e01-e03.avi (no optional info at all)

rules.rule: Wherever `.ext` appears in the documented patterns (the movie file pattern `/Movies/MovieName (release year)/MovieName (release year).ext` and the split/stacked pattern `/Movies/MovieName (release year)/MovieName (release year) - Split_Name.ext`), it is a placeholder: write the file's actual video container extension, for example `.mkv` or `.mp4`, as in `Avatar (2009).mkv` and `Batman Begins (2005).mp4`. Sidecar files are documented with their real extension already, not with `.ext` (for example `Batman Begins (2005).en.srt`), so do not substitute a container extension there. Beware that some operating systems, Windows in particular, hide file extensions by default, so verify the true extension before renaming.

When using the \"Plex TV Series\" agent, Plex recommends always including the year alongside the series title, formatted as \"Title (YYYY)\", in both the show folder name and the episode filename: /Band of Brothers (2001)/Season 01/Band of Brothers (2001) - s01e01 - Currahee.mkv. The year goes on the show folder only, never on the intervening \"Season NN\" folder. This is a recommendation for match quality, not a hard requirement: the page's own examples show /The Office (UK) (2001) {tmdb-2996}/Season 01/The Office (UK) - s01e01 - Downsize.mp4, where the folder carries the year and the filename does not. If a TMDB, TVDB, or IMDb show ID is used, it goes in curly braces after the year, in the folder name only: ShowName (2020) {tmdb-123456}.

A single file covering several consecutive episodes is named ShowName - sXXeYY-eZZ - Optional_Info.ext (first and last episode covered, e.g. s02e18-e19, or Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s02e01-e03.avi). This is a supported naming convention: Plex lists each represented episode individually in the apps, but playing any one of them plays the entire combined file. Plex recommends using a tool to split the video into one file per episode, both so episodes behave truly independently and for a better overall experience, but it is a recommendation rather than a requirement.
examples: s02e01-e03.avi appears as three episode entries; playing episode 2 plays the whole file

rules.rule: Do not confuse the multi-episode range token (one file covering several episodes: ShowName - sXXeYY-eZZ - Optional_Info.ext, e.g. s02e18-e19) with the opposite case of one episode split across several files. For the split case, every part repeats the same single-episode token and carries a stacking name in the trailing field where the optional title would go: ShowName - sXXeYY - Split_Name.ext, where Split_Name is one of cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX or ptX and X is the part number (cd1, cd2, ...). Example: Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s01e01 - pt1.avi and Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s01e01 - pt2.avi. Plex documents only this bare Split_Name form, not a part token appended after an episode title. Stacks are limited to 8 parts, all parts must share the same container and identical audio/subtitle streams in the same order, and Plex explicitly recommends joining the files instead.

With the Plex Movie (non-Legacy) or Plex TV Series agents, subtitle detection is always on and there is no agent setting to configure, so an external subtitle file is picked up only when all three of the following hold: (1) it is a supported format, fully supported being .srt, .smi, .ssa/.ass and .vtt (VOBSUB and PGS may work on some apps but usually force a burn-in transcode), ideally saved as UTF-8; (2) it is named to match the video, Movie_Name (Release Date).[Language_Code].ext for movies and Show_Name SxxEyy.[Language_Code].ext for episodes, where Language_Code is an ISO-639-1 (2-letter) or ISO-639-2/B (3-letter) code, with the optional flags .forced, .sdh or .cc inserted before the extension (SDH/CC needs PMS v1.20.3.3401 or newer and the non-Legacy Plex Movie agent); and (3) it sits beside the video file, or, from server version 1.41.0 with the Plex Movie or Plex Series agents, in a folder named "subs" or "subtitles" in the same parent directory as the video files. Correct: Avatar (2009).en.srt next to Avatar (2009).mkv. Incorrect: subtitles_english.srt, which carries no title, no release date and no valid ISO-639 code. Legacy agents are the exception to the first clause: they additionally require Local Media Assets to be checked in agent settings, plus a "Refresh All Metadata" on the library if it was previously off, and correct naming is still required on top of that.

For movies, the sidecar subtitle filename is the video file's exact base name, then a period, then the language code, then a period, then the subtitle extension: `Movie_Name (Release Date).<Language_Code>.<ext>` (the page writes the placeholder as `[Language_Code]`, and also shows the same name library-relative as `Movies/Movie_Name (Release Date).[Language_Code].ext`; the square brackets are placeholder notation and must NOT appear in the real filename). Components are joined with the ASCII full stop `.`. `<Language_Code>` must be an ISO-639-1 (2-letter) or ISO-639-2/B (3-letter) code, e.g. `Avatar (2009).mkv` -> `Avatar (2009).en.srt` or `Avatar (2009).eng.srt`. Optional flags go between the language code and the extension: `.forced` for forced subtitles, and `.sdh` or `.cc` for deaf/hard-of-hearing or closed-caption tracks (SDH/CC needs Plex Media Server v1.20.3.3401+ and the newer Plex Movie agent, not Plex Movie (Legacy)). Placement: the file normally sits next to the video file (e.g. `/Movies/Avatar (2009)/Avatar (2009).en.srt`); as of server v1.41.0, with the Plex Movie or Plex Series agents, it may instead sit in a folder named `subs` or `subtitles` inside the same parent directory as the video files.

In every documented pattern on the page (Movie_Name (Release Date).[Language_Code].ext, its Movies/-prefixed form, the .forced / .sdh / .cc variants, and TV Shows/Show_Name/Season XX/Show_Name SxxEyy.[Language_Code].ext), the square brackets are the article's typographic marker for a variable and are never part of the filename. Write the bare ISO-639-1 (2-letter) or ISO-639-2/B (3-letter) code as its own dot-delimited segment appended to the media filename's base name, for example Avatar (2009).mkv paired with Avatar (2009).en.srt. Supporting evidence on the page: Movie_Name, Release Date, Show_Name, SxxEyy, XX and ext are placeholders in the same pattern strings written without brackets, and the page glosses them together ("Where [Language_Code] is defined by the ISO-639-1 (2-letter) or ISO-639-2/B (3-letter) standard and ext is the file extension"), so the brackets carry no syntactic meaning. All ten concrete subtitle filenames in the article are bracket-free. Two caveats an implementer needs: the language code is not always the segment immediately before the extension, since an optional forced, sdh or cc flag follows it (Avatar (2009).en.forced.ass, Avatar (2009).en.sdh.srt, Absolutely Fabulous - s02e03.en.forced.smi); and the page shows no incorrect examples at all, so Avatar (2009).[en].srt is a derived illustration of the rule, not a quotation from the source.

The language code is the filename component between the media name and the file extension, and it must be either an ISO-639-1 two-letter code or an ISO-639-2/B three-letter code: "Where [Language_Code] is defined by the ISO-639-1 (2-letter) or ISO-639-2/B (3-letter) standard and ext is the file extension." The same definition applies to movies (Movie_Name (Release Date).[Language_Code].ext) and TV episodes (Show_Name SxxEyy.[Language_Code].ext). Both forms are accepted, and the page's example listings show them side by side within a single folder (Avatar (2009).eng.srt next to Avatar (2009).en.forced.ass and Avatar (2009).de.srt; Absolutely Fabulous - s02e03.eng.smi next to Absolutely Fabulous - s02e03.en.forced.smi), though the page never states in prose that the two forms are interchangeable. Implementation notes: /B is the bibliographic variant, so the three-letter codes are ger, fre, dut, chi rather than the /T forms deu, fra, nld, zho; and an optional flag (forced, sdh, or cc) goes after the language code, as in Movie_Name (Release Date).[Language_Code].forced.ext.

Mark a subtitle as forced by inserting "forced" as its own period-delimited component immediately after the language code and before the extension. Movies: Movie_Name (Release Date).[Language_Code].forced.ext (also valid under a Movies/ folder). TV: the same flag applies, Show_Name SxxEyy.[Language_Code].forced.ext, per "TV content can also make use of 'forced' and 'SDH' subtitles, as outlined for movies." [Language_Code] is required and must be an ISO-639-1 (2-letter) or ISO-639-2/B (3-letter) code; the page shows no forced filename without one.
