Emit the flag lowercase, as every pattern and example on the page does, though the page does not state whether matching is case-sensitive. The "immediately before the extension" placement is documented only for forced used on its own: sdh and cc occupy the same slot (Movie_Name (Release Date).[Language_Code].sdh.ext) and the page never shows forced combined with either, so it defines no ordering for a subtitle that is both forced and SDH.

To mark an external subtitle file as SDH or closed captions, add "sdh" or "cc" as its own period-delimited component between the language code and the file extension, giving "Movie_Name (Release Date).[Language_Code].sdh.ext" or "Movie_Name (Release Date).[Language_Code].cc.ext" (the page shows the token lowercase but states no case requirement). The two tokens are interchangeable alternatives that produce the same SDH/CC track: the page notes that Closed Captioning is "often treated as providing the same type of information" as SDH. The same two pattern lines are shown with an optional "Movies/" prefix, which is the alternate flat-folder location for the sidecar file and is not specific to the cc form. TV episodes follow the same convention: the page states that TV content can also use "forced" and "SDH" subtitles as outlined for movies. Page-verified examples are "Avatar (2009).en.sdh.srt" and "Avatar (2009).de.sdh.srt"; the page shows no cc example, so a cc filename such as "Avatar (2009).en.cc.srt" is inferred from the pattern rather than quoted. Recognition also requires Plex Media Server v1.20.3.3401 or newer and the newer Plex Movie metadata agent, not "Plex Movie (Legacy)".

The `.sdh` and `.cc` subtitle filename flags require Plex Media Server v1.20.3.3401 or newer, plus a current (non-legacy) metadata agent. The page states the agent requirement in its Movies section as the newer Plex Movie agent rather than the older "Plex Movie (Legacy)" agent. Do not generalise that clause to TV: the page says "TV content can also make use of “forced” and “SDH” subtitles, as outlined for movies", and TV libraries use the Plex TV Series agent (the page notes subtitle detection "is always enabled" for the Plex Movie and Plex TV Series agents). So the implementable constraint is: PMS >= 1.20.3.3401 AND the library uses the modern agent for its type (Plex Movie for movies, Plex TV Series for TV), not a Legacy agent.
examples: PMS 1.20.3.3401+ with Plex Movie agent: Avatar (2009).en.sdh.srt is recognised as SDH

rules.rule: For TV, the sidecar sits in the episode's season folder, TV Shows/Show_Name/Season XX/, and its base name is copied from the episode video file character for character, followed by the language code and the subtitle extension. The page's abstract pattern is `TV Shows/Show_Name/Season XX/Show_Name SxxEyy.[Language_Code].ext`, where [Language_Code] is ISO-639-1 (2-letter) or ISO-639-2/B (3-letter) and the square brackets are placeholder notation, not literal characters. Implement the example, not the abstract form: in /TV Shows/Absolutely Fabulous/Season 02/ the video `Absolutely Fabulous - s02e03.avi` takes `Absolutely Fabulous - s02e03.eng.smi`, so the base name carries the video's own " - " separator and lowercase s/e rather than the bullet's "Show_Name SxxEyy" spacing and capitalisation. Optional flags go after the language code and before the extension, giving `<video base>.<lang>.forced.<ext>` (the page's own `Absolutely Fabulous - s02e03.en.forced.smi`) and, since the page says TV supports SDH "as outlined for movies", `<video base>.<lang>.sdh.<ext>` or `.cc.<ext>`; the bare `<base>.<lang>.<ext>` form alone does not cover those. On numbering, the page gives only the placeholders "Season XX" and "SxxEyy" and one zero-padded example (Season 02, s02e03); it does not state padding as a requirement, so treat two-digit zero-padding as the documented convention rather than a quoted rule. Finally, the season folder is not the only documented location: as of server version 1.41.0 with the Plex Series or Plex Movie agents, the identically named subtitle files may instead live in a folder called "subs" or "subtitles" inside that same season folder.

TV episode subtitle filenames use the same [Language_Code] standard as movies, stated separately in the TV Episodes section: ISO-639-1 (2-letter) or ISO-639-2/B (3-letter), in the pattern "TV Shows/Show_Name/Season XX/Show_Name SxxEyy.[Language_Code].ext". Match ISO-639-2/B specifically, the bibliographic variant (ger, fre, chi), not the /T terminology codes (deu, fra, zho). Both widths are valid and may coexist in the same season folder, as in the page's own example where "Absolutely Fabulous - s02e03.eng.smi" sits next to "Absolutely Fabulous - s02e03.en.forced.smi". TV content also accepts the "forced" and "sdh"/"cc" flags after the language code, exactly as documented for movies.

TV episode subtitles use the same flag syntax as movies: the flag token sits immediately after the language code and immediately before the extension, giving "Show_Name SxxEyy.[Language_Code].forced.ext", "Show_Name SxxEyy.[Language_Code].sdh.ext" or "Show_Name SxxEyy.[Language_Code].cc.ext", where [Language_Code] is ISO-639-1 (2-letter) or ISO-639-2/B (3-letter). "cc" is accepted as an equivalent of "sdh". SDH/CC recognition requires Plex Media Server v1.20.3.3401 or newer and the current agent rather than the "(Legacy)" one. Only the forced example is quoted from the page ("Absolutely Fabulous - s02e03.en.forced.smi"); an SDH example such as "Absolutely Fabulous - s02e03.en.sdh.srt" is a valid extrapolation from the movie example "Avatar (2009).en.sdh.srt" and should be labelled as constructed, not cited as page text.

From server version 1.41.0, with the Plex Series or Plex Movie agents (the page names only these two; it does not say other agents are excluded), sidecar subtitle files may live in a subfolder named "subs" or "subtitles" inside the directory that holds the video files rather than beside them. For episodes that means inside the season folder. File names inside the folder follow the normal sidecar naming rules unchanged, including language code and the forced/sdh/cc flags: the page's example moves "Absolutely Fabulous - s01e03.eng.smi" and "Absolutely Fabulous - s02e03.en.forced.smi" into /Subtitles and /Subs without renaming them. The page writes the folder name lowercase in prose but capitalises it as "Subtitles" and "Subs" in its example tree, and says nothing about case matching; treat the name as case-insensitive to satisfy both forms, but note that is inferred from the inconsistency, not documented, and is not guaranteed on a case-sensitive filesystem.

Plex gives full support to four subtitle formats, spanning five extensions: SRT (.srt), SMI (.smi), SSA/ASS (.ssa or .ass) and WebVTT (.vtt). This applies whether they are embedded tracks or external sidecar files. Full support means compatibility with all Plex apps, including clients that require transcoded media. This is not an allow-list for filenames: other formats such as VOBSUB and PGS may still work on some Plex apps, but for the majority they require the video to be transcoded to burn the subtitles in.

Only SRT (.srt), SMI (.smi), SSA/ASS (.ssa or .ass) and WebVTT (.vtt) are fully supported, meaning compatible with all Plex apps including clients that require transcoded media. Other formats such as VOBSUB and PGS may work on some Plex apps but not all, and for the majority of apps they require the video to be transcoded to burn the subtitles in for streaming. Prefer one of the four fully supported formats for any sidecar or embedded subtitle track. (The page does not name file extensions for VOBSUB or PGS; do not cite .sub/.idx/.sup as coming from it.)
examples: VOBSUB (.sub/.idx) and PGS (.sup) trigger burn-in transcoding on most clients

rules.rule: Save external text subtitle files using UTF-8 character encoding. This applies to all supported text subtitle formats (.srt, .smi, .ssa/.ass, .vtt); the page draws no distinction between them. Plex states this as a recommendation rather than a requirement: other encodings may work, but risk strange, unexpected character displays. The page says nothing about byte order marks, so make no claim either way about BOM tolerance.
examples: Write .srt files as UTF-8 (with or without BOM) rather than Windows-1252 or Latin-1

rules.rule: For libraries using a legacy agent, the Local Media Assets source must be enabled per library type and agent (Plex Web App > Settings > select your Plex Media Server > Agents > choose the library type and agent > check Local Media Assets), otherwise local subtitles (embedded or external files) are not picked up. Libraries using the Plex Movie (not "Legacy") or Plex TV Series agent need no agent-settings change, since subtitle detection is always enabled for those agents. If a library previously ran without Local Media Assets enabled, enabling it is not sufficient on its own: the library must also be refreshed with "Refresh All Metadata" to pick up already-scanned local subtitles.
examples: Settings > Server > Agents > (library type) > (agent) > check Local Media Assets

rules.rule: On a library using a legacy agent, enabling the Local Media Assets source only affects items indexed afterwards. If the library did not previously have Local Media Assets enabled, run Refresh All Metadata on it so existing items pick up their embedded subtitles. Libraries using the current Plex Movie or Plex TV Series agents need no agent change, since subtitle detection is always on for those. In Plex Web the action is reached from the library in the navigation sidebar: `...` > Manage Library > Refresh All Metadata (path documented on the linked "Scanning vs Refreshing a Library" article, not on this one).

Keep each major content type in its own dedicated folder tree. The folder you register as a Movie library's content location must contain movie content only, with no TV, music, or other content type under that same path. That folder does not have to sit at the filesystem root: in Plex's own example it is /Media/Movies, alongside /Media/TV Shows and /Media/Music. It is the main folder of each content type (e.g. /Movies, /Music, /TV Shows) that you specify as the content location for that library type. Plex states its scanners and metadata agents "will only work correctly" when the major content types are separated; mixing movie and television content under one path can cause incorrect matching, poorly classified content, and some files being ignored entirely.

The directory specified as a TV library's content location should be a directory that directly contains the individual show folders, not a show folder itself. That directory is normally the top-level content-type folder (e.g. /TV Shows), but it can be a nested category folder when shows are grouped: with /TV Shows/Kids/ShowName vs /TV Shows/Regular/ShowName, /TV Shows/Kids is the source location for a separate "kids" TV library. (Plex phrases this as what you "would typically specify" rather than a hard technical constraint.)
examples: /TV Shows/Kids  (library root for a separate kids library)

rules.rule: Plex matches TV content on the folder structure and the episode filename together, so validate both. The page states: "Both the folder structure and each episode filename must be correct for the best matching experience." Expected layout is <library content location>/<ShowName (Year)>/Season NN/<ShowName (Year)> - sNNeMM - <Optional_Info>.ext, for example /TV Shows/Doctor Who (1963)/Season 01/Doctor Who (1963) - s01e01 - An Unearthly Child.mp4. Folder rules: the library content location is the folder that CONTAINS the individual show folders (not a show folder itself); each show gets its own folder; season folders must use the English word "Season" plus a number even for non-English content; specials are season zero and live in "Season 00" or "Specials". Filename rules: the load-bearing element is the season/episode notation sNNeMM (or a date, YYYY-MM-DD or DD-MM-YYYY, for date-based shows); the separator is free-form, since the page says "It does not matter if you use dashes, dots, or just spaces"; trailing Optional_Info is optional. The year alongside the title in both folder and file names is recommended, not required, and applies to the Plex TV Series agent. Movies and TV must be under separate top-level paths; mixing them "may result in unexpected or incorrect behavior". Practical consequence: treat a correct filename sitting in a missing or misnamed show/season folder as non-conforming, since the page requires both to be correct for reliable matching.

For the "Plex TV Series" agent, Plex recommends (does not require) including the year alongside the series title in both folder and episode file names. Folder: ShowName (Year), the year in round parentheses after a single space, e.g. "Doctor Who (1963)". The parenthesis-and-space format is not stated in prose on the page but is used consistently in every example. The folder name may optionally carry a matching ID appended after the year, in curly braces: ShowName (Year) {tmdb-123456}, {tvdb-123456} or {imdb-tt123456}. Episode files: the recommended form repeats the same ShowName (Year) prefix, e.g. "Band of Brothers (2001) - s01e01 - Currahee.mkv", but this is not universal in the page's own examples: where the folder carries a {tmdb-}/{tvdb-} ID, the article's example filenames drop the year and use ShowName alone ("The Office (UK) - s01e01 - Downsize.mp4"). Treat the year in the filename as recommended, not mandatory. The only element the page treats as genuinely load-bearing is the sXXeXX season and episode notation; the article's generic templates use a bare ShowName with no year at all.
examples: /Band of Brothers (2001)/Season 01/Band of Brothers (2001) - s01e01 - Currahee.mkv
/TV Shows/Doctor Who (1963)/Season 01/Doctor Who (1963) - s01e01 - An Unearthly Child (1).mp4

rules.rule: When using the "Plex TV Series" agent, you may optionally append a TMDB, TVDB, or IMDb show ID to the show FOLDER name, placed after the year and separated by a space. If used, the ID must be enclosed in curly braces in exactly one of the forms {tmdb-123456}, {tvdb-123456}, or {imdb-tt123456}, where 123456 is the show ID. The ID belongs to the show folder only: season folders and episode file names must not carry it (the source's own example folder "The Office (UK) (2001) {tmdb-2996}" contains the file "The Office (UK) - s01e01 - Downsize.mp4", with neither year nor ID). A .plexmatch file is the documented alternative to embedding the ID.

If you are using the "Plex TV Series" agent, you can optionally embed a TMDB, TVDB, or IMDb show ID in the folder name in curly braces to improve matching, for example ShowName (2020) {tmdb-123456}. As an alternative to that, the page points to a .plexmatch file. The page itself gives no placement or format detail and only links to https://support.plex.tv/articles/plexmatch/, which specifies that a .plexmatch file lives in either a series directory or a season directory, and that one at the top level of a series also affects the directories beneath it.

When a season directory is used, it must be named with the English word "Season" followed by the season number, even if the content is in another language. Plex's own examples always capitalize "Season" and zero-pad to two digits (Season 01, Season 02, Season 08), though the page does not explicitly state that padding is mandatory. Season-zero content ("specials") is the only exception to the "Season" wording: it goes in a folder named either "Season 00" or "Specials". A miniseries always uses "Season 01".

For standard season-based shows, each episode filename must contain the season/episode notation sXXeXX, for example s02e17 meaning Season 2 Episode 17. Separators around the marker are free: "It does not matter if you use dashes, dots, or just spaces." The page writes the notation in lowercase and every example on it uses two-digit zero-padded numbers (s01e01, s02e17, s00e01), so emit lowercase zero-padded two-digit values, but note the page states no case-sensitivity or padding requirement, so do not assume shorter or uppercase forms are rejected on input. The rest of the filename is not pure decoration: for the Plex TV Series agent the page recommends always including the series title and year in both folder and file names (e.g. Band of Brothers (2001) - s01e01 - Currahee.mkv), and trailing Optional_Info is ignored only by legacy agents, since the Plex TV Series agent uses it as a matching hint unless it is wrapped in square brackets (e.g. [1080p Bluray]). Folder structure is equally required: /TV Shows/ShowName (Year)/Season NN/, using the English word "Season" regardless of content language, with Season 00 or Specials for season-zero specials, and an optional {tmdb-…}, {tvdb-…} or {imdb-tt…} id in the show folder name. Two variants of the marker exist on the same page: a multi-episode file uses sXXeYY-eZZ (e.g. s02e18-e19), and an episode split across files keeps the same sXXeXX and appends a part suffix from cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX, ptX.
examples: Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s01e02 - The First Cut is the Deepest.avi
From the Earth to the Moon (1998) - s01e01.mp4

rules.rule: The character separating the filename components (title, sXXeXX marker, trailing info) is not fixed. The page states, for season-based shows: "It does not matter if you use dashes, dots, or just spaces." Only those three are named. Underscore is NOT a component separator: the page's own placeholders use it inside a single component (Optional_Info, Split_Name). Plex anchors on the season/episode notation, which the page calls "the most important bit in the file name", but a correct filename alone is not sufficient: the page also requires the /ShowName/Season XX/ folder structure ("Both the folder structure and each episode filename must be correct for the best matching experience"). The trailing info component may be omitted entirely (page example: "Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s01e03.mp4"). The concrete example tree at the end of the article uses ASCII space-hyphen-space throughout, e.g. "Doctor Who (1963) - s01e01 - An Unearthly Child (1).mp4"; the abstract template lines earlier in the article are rendered by Plex's CMS with an en dash (U+2013), e.g. "/TV Shows/ShowName/Season 02/ShowName – s02e17 – Optional_Info.ext", so those templates should not be copied character-for-character. Of the three examples attached to this rule, only "ShowName - s02e17 - Optional_Info.ext" corresponds to a published example; the dot-separated and space-separated forms are extrapolations from the quoted sentence, valid but not printed on the page.

The segment after the sXXeYY marker is what Plex's templates call Optional_Info ("ShowName - sXXeYY - Optional_Info.ext") and it may be omitted entirely; the page's own examples include "From the Earth to the Moon (1998) - s01e01.mp4" and "Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s01e03.mp4" with no trailing segment. Plex states that such optional info "is ignored by Plex when matching content with legacy agents, but it is used in the Plex TV Series agent to give a hint for matching." The page does not prescribe the episode title for that slot, it only labels it Optional_Info, and its own examples put other content there ("- pt1.avi", "- pt2.avi", "An Unearthly Child (1)"). Two consequences follow for a renamer. First, because the TV Series agent reads the segment as a matching hint, put the real episode title there and enclose anything else in square brackets, which Plex ignores by design: "If you want info to be ignored put the optional info in brackets. e.g. /Band of Brothers (2001) - s01e01 - Currahee [1080p Bluray].mkv". Second, the segment is not optional for a split episode, where the page gives a distinct template "ShowName - s02e17 - Split_Name.ext" with Split_Name being one of cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX or ptX; dropping it there makes the parts indistinguishable.
examples: Doctor Who (1963) - s01e01 - An Unearthly Child (1).mp4
Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s00e01 - Straight to the Heart.mkv
From the Earth to the Moon (1998) - s01e02.mp4  (title omitted, still valid)

rules.rule: Anything in the filename that is not part of the show title, season/episode token, or episode title (quality, source, release group, codec) is "Optional_Info" and belongs at the very end of the filename, immediately before the extension, after the episode title when one is present. Legacy agents ignore Optional_Info either way; the Plex TV Series agent otherwise reads it as a matching hint. To stop it being used as a hint, wrap it in square brackets: /Band of Brothers (2001)/Season 01/Band of Brothers (2001) - s01e01 - Currahee [1080p Bluray].mkv. Note that this is separate from show IDs, which the same page requires to be in curly braces in the folder name ({tmdb-123456}, {tvdb-123456}, {imdb-tt123456}).
examples: Band of Brothers (2001) - s01e01 - Currahee [1080p Bluray].mkv

rules.rule: Wherever `.ext` appears in the documented patterns (the movie file pattern `/Movies/MovieName (release year)/MovieName (release year).ext` and the split/stacked pattern `/Movies/MovieName (release year)/MovieName (release year) - Split_Name.ext`), it is a placeholder: write the file's actual video container extension, for example `.mkv` or `.mp4`, as in `Avatar (2009).mkv` and `Batman Begins (2005).mp4`. Sidecar files are documented with their real extension already, not with `.ext` (for example `Batman Begins (2005).en.srt`), so do not substitute a container extension there. Beware that some operating systems, Windows in particular, hide file extensions by default, so verify the true extension before renaming.

Specials belong to season zero. Place them in a folder directly under the show folder named either "Season 00" or "Specials" (the page names these two forms and says nothing about other variants or case), and number the files s00e<episode> with a two-digit episode number, as in "/TV Shows/ShowName/Specials/ShowName - s00e13 - Optional_Info.ext" and "/TV Shows/Grey's Anatomy (2005)/Season 00/Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s00e01 - Straight to the Heart.mkv". Take the episode number from TMDB's listing for that special rather than assigning your own; if unsure whether an episode is a special, check it on TMDB and name it as shown there. If the item does not appear on TMDB at all (DVD special, behind the scenes, goof reel), do not give it an s00e number: add it as an "extra" for the show instead, per the Plex TV extras article.
examples: /TV Shows/Grey's Anatomy (2005)/Season 00/Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s00e01 - Straight to the Heart.mkv

rules.rule: Specials belong to season zero: put them in a folder named either "Season 00" or "Specials" and number them s00eNN (e.g. /TV Shows/ShowName/Specials/ShowName - s00e13 - Optional_Info.ext). If you are unsure whether a particular episode is a Special, check the episode on TMDB and name it as you see it there. If a special you have does not appear on TMDB at all (a DVD special, behind the scenes, goof reel, and so on), Plex suggests adding the item as a TV "extra" for the show instead of giving it an s00eNN slot; see the Plex article on local files for TV show trailers and extras.
examples: Behind-the-scenes reel -> add as an extra, not /Season 00/

rules.rule: Date-based shows are shown inside a Season folder, with the sXXeXX marker replaced by the air date: /TV Shows/ShowName/Season NN/ShowName - DATE - Optional_Info.ext (the page's templates write \"Season 02\" as a placeholder; the worked example uses Season 08, so use the show's actual season number). The date may be in either YYYY-MM-DD or DD-MM-YYYY order, and its internal separator may be a dash (2011-11-15), a period (2011.11.15) or a space (2011 11 15). The delimiter surrounding the date is separate from that internal separator: the page's templates use a spaced en dash and its concrete example uses a spaced hyphen, as in /TV Shows/The Colbert Report (2005)/Season 08/The Colbert Report (2005) - 2011-11-15 - Elijah Wood.avi. Note the page shows every date-based example inside a Season folder but never states in words that the folder is mandatory.
examples: /TV Shows/The Colbert Report (2005)/Season 08/The Colbert Report (2005) - 2011-11-15 - Elijah Wood.avi

rules.rule: Name a show the way it is numbered by your metadata source: season-based shows use SxxExx, date-based shows use an air date. When you cannot tell which a show is, look it up on The Movie Database (TMDB) or The TVDB and follow whichever form it uses there. Date-based episodes still go inside a "Season NN" folder, exactly like season-based ones. Only the episode identifier changes, for example /TV Shows/The Colbert Report (2005)/Season 08/The Colbert Report (2005) - 2011-11-15 - Elijah Wood.avi. The date may be written YYYY-MM-DD or DD-MM-YYYY, with dashes, periods, or spaces as separators.
examples: The Colbert Report -> date-based on TMDB -> ShowName (Year) - 2011-11-15 - Title.avi

rules.rule: A miniseries is handled just like a season-based show: put every regular episode in a single "Season 01" folder and use s01exx notation in the filename (/TV Shows/ShowName (Year)/Season 01/ShowName (Year) - s01e01 - Optional_Info.ext). The separator between title, episode code and optional info is free-form (dashes, dots or spaces all work), and including the year in the folder and file name is a recommendation of the Plex TV Series agent rather than a miniseries-specific requirement. The Specials rule still overrides: any special belongs in "Season 00" or "Specials" with s00exx, not in Season 01.
examples: /TV Shows/From the Earth to the Moon (1998)/Season 01/From the Earth to the Moon (1998) - s01e01.mp4

rules.rule: A single file covering two or more consecutive episodes uses the range form s<season>e<first>-e<last>, placed in the matching "Season NN" folder for that season. The season prefix appears once, then the first episode number, then a hyphen, then "e" plus the last episode number. Season and episode numbers are written as two digits, zero-padded (Plex's own examples are s02e18-e19 and s02e01-e03). Full form per the page: /TV Shows/ShowName/Season 02/ShowName - sXXeYY-eZZ - Optional_Info.ext, e.g. /TV Shows/Grey's Anatomy (2005)/Season 02/Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s02e01-e03.avi. The separators around the notation (dashes, dots, spaces) are flexible, but the "-e" joining the two episode numbers is not.

Multi-episode files are supported. Name them /TV Shows/ShowName/Season 02/ShowName - sXXeYY-eZZ - Optional_Info.ext, where YY is the first and ZZ the last episode covered by the file (page example: s02e18-e19; example tree: "Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s02e01-e03.avi"). Such files show up as individual episodes in Plex apps, but playing any of the represented episodes plays the full file, so Plex recommends using a tool to split the video into one file per episode if you want episodes to behave truly independently. This is a recommendation, not a restriction: unlike the "Episodes Split Across Multiple Files" section, it carries no warning about degraded features, so a renamer should preserve and correctly emit the sXXeYY-eZZ form and at most surface the split suggestion, never rewrite or reject the file.
examples: Split Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s02e01-e03.avi into s02e01.avi, s02e02.avi, s02e03.avi

rules.rule: Files that together make up a single episode share an identical "ShowName - sXXeYY" prefix and differ only in a trailing part token, which must be one of cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX or ptX with X replaced by the part number counting from 1 (cd1, cd2, and so on). The part token occupies the optional-title slot, so a stacked part carries no episode title: "ShowName - s02e17 - pt1.ext". Plex's placeholder template renders the separators as en dashes, but its worked example uses space-hyphen-space ("Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s01e01 - pt1.avi"), which is the form an implementation should produce. Additional constraints stated on the same page: a stack supports at most 8 parts, every part must use the same file format (all MP4 or all MKV), and all parts should have identical audio and subtitle streams in the same order. Plex warns that split files are not the expected way to handle content, that not all apps support playback of them, and recommends joining the files instead.
examples: cd1 / disc1 / disk1 / dvd1 / part1 / pt1

rules.rule: Split parts are named `ShowName - s02e17 - <Split_Name>.ext` where Split_Name is one of `cdX`, `discX`, `diskX`, `dvdX`, `partX`, `ptX` and X is the part number starting at 1 (cd1, cd2, ...). Constraints from the page: all parts MUST be of the same file format (e.g. all MP4 or all MKV); all parts SHOULD have identical audio and subtitle streams in the same order (stated as a recommendation, not a hard requirement); only stacks up to 8 parts are supported. The page also warns that not all Plex apps support playback of split media, and recommends joining the files into a single video instead.

Episode order (aired, DVD, absolute, and regional variants) is chosen in Plex settings, never written into a filename: there is no filename token for it. Set the library default under the Advanced tab when creating or editing the TV library, where the Plex TV Series agent defaults to TMDB order, which is an aired order. Set a per-show override under the Advanced tab when editing that show, which requires Plex Media Server 1.40.4 or later, the Plex TV Series agent, and a show that has already been successfully matched; the per-show choices are the alternate orders The TVDB publishes for that series. The setting and the filenames must agree: the sXXeXX numbers in the filename have to follow whichever order is selected, so pick the order your files are already numbered against. Options commonly offered include "The Movie Database (Aired)", "TheTVDB (Aired)", "TheTVDB (DVD)" and "TheTVDB (Absolute)", but the list is not exhaustive and varies per show, for example "TheTVDB (US)".

The article mentions anime exactly once, as a passing illustration inside the "Episode Ordering" section: "For instance, some people like to handle anime series as a single season, using “Absolute” series order." It does not prescribe this and gives no anime example. "Absolute" is an ordering setting, never a filename format: the page supplies no absolute-numbering filename syntax at all, and its only naming syntaxes are sXXeXX for season-based shows, the date-based forms, s00eXX inside Season 00 or Specials, and sXXeYY-eZZ for multi-episode files. Naming absolute-order files with a normal sXXeYY marker inside a single Season folder therefore follows by inference from the absence of any alternative, not from a stated rule. Selecting "TheTVDB (Absolute)" is a per-show action: it appears only in the per-show "Episode ordering" list under "Alternate orders", which requires Plex Media Server 1.40.4 or newer with the Plex TV Series agent, works only after the show has been successfully matched, and is set from the Advanced tab when editing the show. The page notes shows "will most commonly have one or more of these options", so Absolute is not guaranteed to be offered for a given series. The separate library-level Episode Ordering preference under "Setting the Library Default Ordering" is only a TMDB-versus-TVDB choice and is not where Absolute is picked.
examples: /TV Shows/ShowName (Year)/Season 01/ShowName (Year) - s01e123 - Title.mkv with per-show ordering set to TheTVDB (Absolute)

rules.rule: Keep each major content type in its own separate main directory, used as that library's root, rather than mixing types under one directory. Plex explicitly and strongly recommends this for movie versus television content, and frames it generally as keeping "major types of content separated from each other"; the page's example nests the roots under a shared parent, e.g. /Media/Movies, /Media/Music, /Media/TV Shows, but neither the parent name nor that exact layout is required. This is a strong recommendation, not a hard requirement: Plex "will do its best" to match content anyway, but the page warns that failure to separate content such as movies and TV shows "may result in unexpected or incorrect behavior".

For libraries using the new Plex Movie agent, enable \"Use local Assets\" in the library's advanced settings. That single toggle is the whole agent-side configuration needed for Plex to load local media assets (posters, clear logos, background/fanart, square art, external subtitles, and local trailers/extras); unlike the legacy Personal Media, Plex Movie (Legacy) and The Movie Database agents, there is no separate \"Local Media Assets\" agent source to check and move to the top of the list under Settings > Server > Agents. The files themselves must still be named and organized per Plex's naming conventions.
examples: Library > Advanced settings > Use local Assets = on

rules.rule: For libraries using the legacy Personal Media, Plex Movie (Legacy) or The Movie Database agents, local assets (posters, backgrounds, subtitles, extras) are only picked up if the "Local Media Assets" agent source is both checked and topmost in that agent's source list: Settings > (your Plex Media Server) > Agents > choose the Library Type (e.g. Movies) and the Agent (e.g. Plex Movie (Legacy)), then ensure Local Media Assets is checked and topmost. This does not apply to the current Plex Movie agent, where you instead enable "Use local Assets" in the library's advanced settings.
examples: Settings > Server > Agents > Movies > Plex Movie (Legacy) > Local Media Assets checked and first in list

rules.rule: Local ARTWORK image files must use one of exactly four extensions: jpg, jpeg, png, or tbn. Source: "Local Artwork Assets" > "Supported Artwork Image Formats" ("The supported image file formats are: jpg, jpeg, png, tbn"). This applies to the .ext placeholder in the artwork sections only: Poster Artwork (MovieName (Release Date).ext, Custom_Poster_Name.ext where the name is cover/default/folder/movie/poster, and Custom_Poster_Name-X.ext), Clear Logos (clearlogo.ext, logo.ext, clearlogo-X.ext, logo-X.ext), Background/Fanart (MovieName (Release Date)-fanart.ext, Custom_Fanart_Name.ext where the name is art/backdrop/background/fanart, and Custom_Fanart_Name-X.ext), and Square Art (square.ext, squareArt.ext, backgroundSquare.ext). It does NOT apply to every .ext on the page: in "External Subtitle Files", MovieName (Release Date).[Language_Code].ext and ...forced.ext take a subtitle extension (SRT, SMI, SSA/ASS), not an image one. Also note the article recommends PNG specifically for clear logos, because the alpha channel allows a transparent surround.

A poster stored beside the movie file, rather than inside a per-movie folder, is detected when its base name matches the movie file's base name, in the form "MovieName (Release Date).ext": title, one space, release date in round parentheses. The page's flat example is "/Movies/Batman Begins (2005).mkv" with "Batman Begins (2005)-1.jpg" and "Batman Begins (2005)-2.tbn" alongside it, so the base name may additionally carry a "-X" numeric suffix when more than one poster is supplied. "ext" must be one of jpg, jpeg, png or tbn. Every release date the page shows is a 4-digit year. The alternative storage form is the per-movie folder one, "Movie/MovieName (Release Date)/Custom_Poster_Name.ext", where Custom_Poster_Name is cover, default, folder, movie or poster.

A poster inside a per-movie folder (Movie/MovieName (Release Date)/) must have a base filename of cover, default, folder, movie, or poster, optionally followed by a numeric suffix of the form -X for additional selectable posters (for example poster-2.png), and one of the supported image extensions: jpg, jpeg, png, or tbn. This per-folder form is one of two documented placements; the alternative applies when the movie file sits directly in the library root rather than in its own folder, where the poster is instead named after the movie file itself as MovieName (Release Date).ext, with MovieName (Release Date)-X.ext for additional posters.

Additional posters are named by appending a hyphen and a number to an accepted poster base name. Inside a movie folder the base name is one of the page's five accepted values (cover, default, folder, movie, poster), giving "Custom_Poster_Name-X.ext"; beside a loose movie file the base name is the movie's own "MovieName (Release Date)", giving "MovieName (Release Date)-X.ext". The page states only "Where -X is a number" and shows 1 and 2, so no zero padding, no starting value, and no upper bound are specified. The page's example shows the first poster may be either unnumbered (poster.jpg next to poster-2.png) or numbered from 1 (Batman Begins (2005)-1.jpg next to Batman Begins (2005)-2.tbn), so a number on the first file is not required. Extensions may differ between the numbered variants, each drawn from the supported set jpg, jpeg, png, tbn. Which one is displayed is chosen in the Plex Web App.

Poster artwork is typically 1:1.5 aspect ratio (width:height, i.e. taller than wide). This is descriptive guidance only: the page states it with "typically" and never expresses it as a requirement. Plex detects a poster by filename and location alone (MovieName (Release Date).ext, or cover/default/folder/movie/poster plus an image extension inside the movie folder), so image dimensions are never a matching or validation criterion. The page specifies no pixel dimensions for posters and no minimum or recommended size, so a renamer must not validate, warn on, or reject poster files based on their aspect ratio or resolution. Examples: none available from this source (the page gives no pixel sizes; the commonly cited 1000 x 1500 px figure does not appear on it). For contrast, the same page states background/fanart artwork "typically uses a 16:9 aspect ratio", equally descriptive.

A background image placed directly beside the movie file (rather than in a per-movie folder) is named with the movie's "MovieName (Release Date)" base name plus a "-fanart" suffix before the extension: /Movies/Avatar (2009)-fanart.jpg beside /Movies/Avatar (2009).mkv. Three qualifications the page makes explicit. First, this sibling form is one of two documented alternatives; the other gives the movie its own folder and names the image with a bare Custom_Fanart_Name, one of art, backdrop, background, or fanart, as in /Movies/Avatar (2009)/fanart.jpg. Second, those alternative names (art, backdrop, background) are documented only as bare filenames inside the per-movie folder; the page writes the sibling suffix as the literal "-fanart" and does not document "-art", "-backdrop", or "-background" siblings. Contrast the Square Art section, where the sibling form is written parameterized as "MovieName (Release Date)-Custom_SquareArt_Name.ext". Third, "-fanart.ext" is the single-image sibling form, not the only legal sibling name: for more than one background beside the movie file the page appends a number, "MovieName (Release Date)-fanart-X.ext", shown as /Movies/Batman Begins (2005)-fanart-1.jpg and /Movies/Batman Begins (2005)-fanart-2.tbn beside /Movies/Batman Begins (2005).mkv. A matcher should therefore accept the base name followed by "-fanart" optionally followed by "-" plus a number, then the extension. Extensions are not enumerated for fanart; the page's examples use .jpg, .png, and .tbn.

Inside a per-movie folder, a background (fanart) image must be named either `<name>.ext` or `<name>-X.ext`, where `<name>` is exactly one of art, backdrop, background, or fanart; `-X` is a number used to distinguish multiple fanart images, which the Plex Web App then lets you choose between; and `ext` is one of jpg, jpeg, png, or tbn. Example valid names in /Movies/Avatar (2009)/: fanart.jpg, fanart-2.png, art.png, backdrop.jpg, background.tbn. (Separately, the page documents a second form attached to the video file itself, `MovieName (Release Date)-fanart.ext` and `MovieName (Release Date)-fanart-X.ext`, which its examples show for videos stored without a per-movie folder.)

Additional background images append a hyphen plus a number to the accepted base name. Inside a movie folder the page states the pattern as "Custom_Fanart_Name-X.ext", where Custom_Fanart_Name is one of art, backdrop, background or fanart; beside the movie file the page gives no prose pattern but its example uses "MovieName (Release Date)-fanart-X.ext". "Where -X is a number" is the page's only constraint: it states no start index, no zero padding and no maximum. Its own examples are inconsistent about the start, the folder case pairing an unnumbered fanart.jpg with fanart-2.png while the sidecar case starts at -fanart-1.jpg, so an unnumbered base file and numbered siblings can coexist and a parser should accept numbering from either 1 or 2.

Background (fanart) artwork typically uses a 16:9 aspect ratio. The page states this descriptively ("typically") and enforces nothing: it gives no pixel dimensions, no minimum resolution, and no aspect-ratio check. Whether a fanart file is detected depends only on its name, either "MovieName (Release Date)-fanart.ext" or a file named art, backdrop, background or fanart inside "Movies/MovieName (Release Date)/". Treat any concrete size such as 1920x1080 as an illustration of 16:9, not as page-sourced guidance.

Clear logo art uses the base name "clearlogo" or "logo" with a supported image extension (jpg, jpeg, png, tbn; PNG recommended because its alpha channel lets the backdrop show through). Two accepted layouts: beside the movie file as "MovieName (Release Date)-clearlogo.ext" (the page's only sidecar example is "Avatar (2009)-clearlogo.png"; a "-logo" sidecar suffix is not shown and should not be assumed), or inside the per-movie folder as "clearlogo.ext" or "logo.ext". Multiple logos are supported as "clearlogo-X.ext" / "logo-X.ext" where -X is a number, so "clearlogo-1.png" and "clearlogo-2.png" can sit alongside "clearlogo.png" in the movie folder. Ignore the line "TV Shows/Movie Name (year)/clearlogo.png" that appears in this section: it is a copy-paste artifact from the TV Shows article, not a movie path.

Clear logo files (clearlogo.ext or logo.ext, plus the numbered clearlogo-X.ext / logo-X.ext variants for multiple logos) should preferably use PNG, because PNG supports a transparent surrounding area (alpha channel) that lets the image or colors behind it show through. PNG is recommended, not required: any supported artwork format (jpg, jpeg, png, tbn) is accepted, so when several candidates exist, rank .png above the others rather than rejecting them.

Additional clear logos are named by appending a hyphen and a number to the base name, giving "clearlogo-X.ext" or "logo-X.ext". The page states only "Where -X is a number"; its examples use the integers 1 and 2, so treat X as a positive integer. The unnumbered "clearlogo.ext" may sit alongside the numbered files (the page's example lists clearlogo.png, clearlogo-1.png and clearlogo-2.png together in /Movies/Avatar (2009)/), and the selection among them is made in the Plex Web App. The page documents this numbering only for the in-folder base names clearlogo/logo; it never shows a numbered form of the flat "MovieName (year)-clearlogo.ext" variant.

Square art (the background image used on the details screens of movies in the iOS and Android mobile apps) is matched by three base names, spelled on the page as square, squareArt and backgroundSquare. Place the image either beside the movie file, named "MovieName (Release Date)-<name>.ext" where the part before the dash is the movie file's own base name, or inside the per-movie folder as "<name>.ext". The extension must be one of the page's supported artwork formats: jpg, jpeg, png, tbn. The page prints the names in camel case but never states whether matching is case sensitive, so write them as documented and do not rely on case insensitivity. All local asset naming requires local assets to be enabled for the library: "Local Media Assets" checked and topmost in the agent source list for legacy agents, or "Use local assets" in advanced settings for the new Plex Movie agent.

External subtitle files picked up by the Local Media Assets scanner are SRT, SMI, and SSA (or ASS); the file still has to follow the naming pattern MovieName (Release Date).[Language_Code].ext (optionally .forced before the extension) to be detected with a language. Other formats, such as VOBSUB, PGS and similar, may work on some Plex apps but not all.

An external subtitle file takes the movie file's base name, then a dot, then the language code, then the subtitle extension: `MovieName (Release Date).<lang>.ext`, where `<lang>` is an ISO-639-1 (2-letter) or ISO-639-2/B (3-letter) code. It may sit beside the movie file directly under the library folder, or inside the movie's own folder alongside the video. An optional `forced` tag may follow the language code, giving `MovieName (Release Date).<lang>.forced.ext`; that tag makes the subtitle enabled even when it does not match the server's language settings, and is normally used for tracks that only translate foreign-language parts. Components are separated by literal dots, and the square brackets in Plex's written pattern are placeholders, never literal characters, as the page's own examples show: `Avatar (2009).en.srt` and `Avatar (2009).eng.ass`. Omitting the language code does not stop the file being picked up, but Plex then labels the track "Unknown" and automatic subtitle selection will not work as intended, so always write it. The scanner supports SRT, SMI and SSA (or ASS); other formats such as VOBSUB or PGS may work on some Plex apps but not all.

Insert the literal token ".forced" between the language code and the file extension: "MovieName (Release Date).[Language_Code].forced.ext" (the page shows it as "Movies/MovieName (Release Date).[Language_Code].forced.ext"). The language code is still required and must be ISO-639-1 (2-letter) or ISO-639-2/B (3-letter); without it Plex shows "Unknown" and its automatic subtitle-selection logic will not work as intended. Effect, per the page: "forced" is a special tag which makes the subtitle enabled even if it does not necessarily follow the rules set in your server's language settings, normally used for subs which only contain the translation for foreign parts. Do not describe it as overriding language settings outright. Note that the page prints no forced example; "Movies/Avatar (2009).en.forced.srt" is a derived example, not a quoted one.

Include a language code in every external subtitle filename, placed between the movie name and the extension: "MovieName (Release Date).[Language_Code].ext" (optionally "...[Language_Code].forced.ext"), where [Language_Code] is ISO-639-1 (2-letter) or ISO-639-2/B (3-letter). The file is still picked up without a code, but Plex apps show "Unknown" instead of the subtitle language and the automatic process that decides whether the subtitle should be shown does not work as intended. Right: /Movies/Avatar (2009).en.srt or /Movies/Avatar (2009)/Avatar (2009).eng.ass. Wrong: /Movies/Avatar (2009).srt.

A movie inline extra is a video file placed in the movie's own directory, alongside the main movie file:

Movies/<MovieName> (<Release Date>)/<Descriptive_Name>-<Extra_Type>.ext

The filename must END with a hyphen followed by one of exactly eight extra-type tokens: -behindthescenes, -deleted, -featurette, -interview, -scene, -short, -trailer, -other. Plex's wording: "The filename must end in the -Extra_Type value exactly. The hyphen is important and you cannot have spaces between the hyphen and word." So the delimiter is the LAST hyphen in the stem; the descriptive part before it may itself contain hyphens, spaces, and punctuation (the page's own examples include "Theatrical Trailer #1-trailer.mp4"). A descriptive name before the type is recommended, not required by the stated pattern.

The containing directory is the movie's directory, named "<MovieName> (<Release Date>)" (example: "Avatar (2009)"), and it holds the main movie file (example: "Avatar (2009).mkv"). Inline extras are only valid when that directory contains a single main movie file plus local assets such as artwork and subtitles; with multiple versions of the movie in one directory, Plex requires the "Organized in Subdirectories" form instead (Movies/MovieName (Release Date)/<Extra_Directory_Type>/<Descriptive_name>.ext). Extras added after the movie is already in the library generally need a Refresh Metadata to be picked up, and the Local Media Assets source must be enabled.

For a movie extra placed inline (in the same directory as the movie, named "MovieName (Release Date)"), the filename must follow "Descriptive_Name-Extra_Type.ext": a descriptive name, then the extra-type token as the final part of the filename immediately before the extension. The page documents the token in lowercase with a leading hyphen and no space between the hyphen and the word, and states the filename must end in the -Extra_Type value exactly. The permitted tokens are exactly these eight: -behindthescenes, -deleted, -featurette, -interview, -scene, -short, -trailer, -other. The title-cased, spaced names (Behind The Scenes, Deleted Scenes, Featurettes, Interviews, Scenes, Shorts, Trailers, Other) are the separate "Organized in Subdirectories" method and are not valid inline filename suffixes.

Applies to the inline naming method only, meaning an extra stored alongside the movie file or the episode file. The filename stem must end with the extra-type suffix: a hyphen immediately followed by one of behindthescenes, deleted, featurette, interview, scene, short, trailer, other, with no space between the hyphen and the word and nothing after the word except the file extension. Source, identical on the movie and TV extras pages: "The filename must end in the -Extra_Type value exactly. The hyphen is important and you cannot have spaces between the hyphen and word." One documented exception, stated on the TV page: a numeric index may be appended directly to the token to hold several extras of the same type for one episode (Game of Thrones - S01E01 - Winter is Coming-deleted1.mkv, -deleted2.mkv, -deleted3.mkv), so a trailing integer immediately after the token is valid and must not be stripped. This rule does not apply to extras organized in subdirectories (Behind The Scenes, Deleted Scenes, Featurettes, Interviews, Scenes, Shorts, Trailers, Other), where the file carries a plain descriptive name and no suffix. Neither page specifies letter case, so do not enforce case sensitivity on the token.

A movie extra organised by subdirectory goes at Movies/<MovieName> (<Release Date>)/<Extra_Directory_Type>/<Descriptive_name>.ext, exactly one directory level below the movie's own folder, with no -Extra_Type suffix needed on the filename because the folder name carries the type instead. <Extra_Directory_Type> must be one of exactly eight names, spelled and capitalised as: Behind The Scenes, Deleted Scenes, Featurettes, Interviews, Scenes, Shorts, Trailers, Other. A descriptive filename is recommended, not required. For a multi-edition movie, the "movie's own folder" is the specific edition folder and the extras go inside it. Detection additionally requires the Local Media Assets agent source to be enabled (or "Use local Assets" in the library's advanced settings under the current Plex Movie agent), and a Refresh Metadata on the movie when extras are added after it was already scanned. The page documents this subdirectory method for movies only.

For movies, the "Organized in Subdirectories" method places extras at Movies/MovieName (Release Date)/Extra_Directory_Type/Descriptive_name.ext, where Extra_Directory_Type is one of the eight names the page enumerates: Behind The Scenes, Deleted Scenes, Featurettes, Interviews, Scenes, Shorts, Trailers, Other. Write them in that exact Title Case with single spaces, capital "The" in "Behind The Scenes", matching both the enumerated list and the worked example tree. The page presents this as a closed list but does not itself state that the directory names are case-sensitive, so treat the Title Case spelling as the documented canonical form to emit when renaming, and do not claim the article forbids other casings. This list governs subdirectory names only; the page's alternative inline method instead keeps extras beside the movie file with a filename suffix (-behindthescenes, -deleted, -featurette, -interview, -scene, -short, -trailer, -other), and there the article does require the filename to end in the suffix exactly, with no space around the hyphen. Scope is movie libraries; this article says nothing about TV show or season extras.

Movie extras must use one of exactly two layouts, and both live inside a directory named for the movie (for a multi-edition movie, inside that specific edition's own named directory): (1) Inline, in the same directory as the main movie file, where each extra's filename ends exactly in one of -behindthescenes, -deleted, -featurette, -interview, -scene, -short, -trailer, or -other (the hyphen is required and there is no space between the hyphen and the word), giving Movies/MovieName (Release Date)/Descriptive_Name-Extra_Type.ext; or (2) In a direct subdirectory of the movie's directory whose name is exactly one of Behind The Scenes, Deleted Scenes, Featurettes, Interviews, Scenes, Shorts, Trailers, or Other, with any descriptive filename inside, giving Movies/MovieName (Release Date)/Extra_Directory_Type/Descriptive_name.ext. The inline layout additionally requires that the movie directory hold only the one main movie file plus the extras and other local assets such as artwork or subtitles; if multiple versions of the movie share the directory, the subdirectory layout must be used instead. Detection also depends on the library having the Local Media Assets source enabled (or "Use local assets" on the current Plex Movie agent), and extras added after the movie is already in the library generally need a Refresh Metadata to be picked up.

Inline extras method: apart from the extras themselves, the movie's directory may contain only the main movie file plus other local media assets such as artwork or subtitles. In practice this means at most one non-suffixed video file in Movies/MovieName (Release Date)/, with every other video file carrying an -Extra_Type suffix. If two or more versions of the movie sit together in that directory, do not use inline extras; use the "Organized in Subdirectories" method instead, naming files as Movies/MovieName (Release Date)/Extra_Directory_Type/Descriptive_name.ext where Extra_Directory_Type is one of Behind The Scenes, Deleted Scenes, Featurettes, Interviews, Scenes, Shorts, Trailers, Other. Source quote: "Besides the extras themselves, you can only have the main movie file (or other local media assets like artwork or subtitles) in the directory. If you have multiple versions of the movie together, use the “Organized in Subdirectories” method below."
examples: Multiple versions present, so use /Movies/Avatar (2009)/Trailers/… rather than inline suffixed files

rules.rule: When a movie has multiple editions, each edition must be stored in its own named movie directory (see Plex's "Naming and organizing your Movie files" article for how that directory is named). An edition's local trailers and extras can then be placed inside that specific edition folder using either of the two normal methods: inline as MovieName (Release Date)/Descriptive_Name-Extra_Type.ext, or in a subdirectory as MovieName (Release Date)/Extra_Directory_Type/Descriptive_name.ext. The page does not state where extras placed outside an edition folder end up, so treat "not in a shared parent" as an implication of per-edition placement rather than a documented rule.
examples: extras placed inside the specific edition folder, not in a shared parent

rules.rule: Plex recommends, but does not require, a descriptive name for an extra. Inline, that name goes before the type suffix ("It is recommended that you provide some sort of descriptive name for the extra before specifying the type at the end of the filename."), e.g. "Performance Capture-behindthescenes.mkv"; note the suffix itself is mandatory, since "The filename must end in the -Extra_Type value exactly", so the descriptive part may be weak but cannot be absent. In the subdirectory scheme the descriptive name is the whole filename, covered by a separate sentence ("It is recommended that you provide some sort of descriptive name for the extras filenames."), e.g. "Trailers/Theatrical Trailer #2.mp4". Treat a missing or non-descriptive name as a warning, never an error.

Local movie extras are only picked up when the local-assets source is active for the library. With the current Plex Movie agent, enable "Use local Assets" in the library's advanced settings. With the Personal Media, Plex Movie (Legacy) and The Movie Database legacy agents, go to Plex Web App > Settings > (your Plex Media Server) > Agents, select the library type and agent, then ensure "Local Media Assets" is checked and topmost in the agent source list. Note the two settings live in different places: the Plex Movie agent toggle is per-library advanced settings, the legacy source ordering is on the server-level Agents screen. Extras must also be named and organized correctly; enabling the source alone is not sufficient. When extras are added after the movie is already in the library, run Refresh Metadata on that movie.
examples: Plex Movie agent: enable “Use local Assets” in advanced settings
Legacy agents: check Local Media Assets and move it to the top of the list

rules.rule: For movies only (this article covers movie extras, not TV shows): when extras are added to a movie that is already in the Plex library, you will likely need to trigger the Refresh Metadata action on that movie for Plex to pick up the new files. This applies to both the inline naming method and the extras subdirectory method (Behind The Scenes, Deleted Scenes, Featurettes, Interviews, Scenes, Shorts, Trailers, Other).
examples: Refresh Metadata on Avatar (2009) after adding Trailers/

rules.rule: Movie and television content must be kept in separate top-level directories; mixing them can produce incorrect matching.
TV show extras organised by subdirectory go at <TV Show> (<Release Date>)/<Extra_Directory_Type>/<Descriptive_name>.ext, i.e. an extras-type folder directly inside the show's own directory.

For TV shows the extras subdirectory name must be exactly one of the same eight Title Case names used for movies: Behind The Scenes, Deleted Scenes, Featurettes, Interviews, Scenes, Shorts, Trailers, Other.

Season-level extras live in an extras-type subdirectory placed inside that season's own directory (<Show>/<Season NN>/<Extra_Directory_Type>/<Descriptive_name>.ext), while show-level extras sit in an extras-type subdirectory directly under the show directory.
examples: season level: /Game of Thrones/Season 01/Behind The Scenes/A look at season 1.mkv
season level: /Game of Thrones/Season 01/Deleted Scenes/Season 1 Deleted Scenes.mkv

rules.rule: A show-level extra may also be placed inline directly in the show's root directory using the hyphen-plus-type suffix, without any extras subfolder.
examples: /Game of Thrones/An Interview With Emilia Clarke-interview.mkv

rules.rule: An episode extra is placed in the same season directory as the episode and is named identically to the episode file with the extra-type suffix appended to the stem: <Show> - S<NN>E<NN> - <Episode Title>-<Extra_Type>.ext.
examples: Game of Thrones - S01E01 - Winter is Coming.mkv
Game of Thrones - S01E01 - Winter is Coming-deleted.mkv
Game of Thrones - S01E01 - Winter is Coming-featurette.mkv

rules.rule: For TV episode extras the suffix must be exactly one of the same eight lowercase hyphen-prefixed tokens as movies: -behindthescenes, -deleted, -featurette, -interview, -scene, -short, -trailer, -other.
To attach several episode extras of the same type, append a numeric index directly to the end of the suffix with no separator (for example -deleted1, -deleted2, -deleted3).
examples: Game of Thrones - S01E01 - Winter is Coming-deleted1.mkv
Game of Thrones - S01E01 - Winter is Coming-deleted2.mkv
Game of Thrones - S01E01 - Winter is Coming-deleted3.mkv

rules.rule: TV extras must use one of exactly two layouts: inline in the same season directory as the episode, or in a subdirectory of the main TV show directory.
examples: inline: /Game of Thrones/Season 01/Game of Thrones - S01E01 - Winter is Coming-deleted.mkv
subdirectory: /Game of Thrones/Season 01/Deleted Scenes/Season 1 Deleted Scenes.mkv

rules.rule: Local TV trailers and extras are documented as working when the Plex TV Series agent is in use.
examples: TV library configured with the Plex TV Series agent

rules.rule: After adding TV extras to a show, season or episode that already exists in the library, trigger Refresh Metadata on the show as a whole.
examples: Refresh Metadata on Game of Thrones after adding /Season 01/Deleted Scenes/

rules.rule: TV extras are not equally visible on all clients: only the iOS and Android mobile apps fully support extras at show, season and episode level, so absence of an extra in a given client is not proof of a naming error.
examples: Plex Web and Desktop are listed as supporting only one of the three levels

rules.rule: Local artwork files must use one of exactly four image file extensions: jpg, jpeg, png, or tbn.

Local asset loading must be switched on for the library before any of these files are read: with the new Plex TV Series agent, enable "Use local Assets" in the library settings; with the legacy TheTVDB, TheMovieDB or Personal Media Shows agents, the "Local Media Assets" agent source must be checked and placed topmost in the agent source list.
examples: Settings > server > Agents > Shows > (agent) > Local Media Assets checked and topmost in the list

rules.rule: Keep movie and television content in separate top-level directories (for example /Media/Movies and /Media/TV Shows) rather than mixed in one folder.
A series-level poster is an image placed directly in the show's folder whose base name is exactly one of: folder, poster, or show, followed by a supported image extension.
Additional series posters use the same base name followed by a hyphen and a number, as Custom_ShowPoster_Name-X.ext, where X is a number; which one is used is then selected in the Plex Web App.
A clear logo (show title art) is an image placed inside the show folder named exactly clearlogo.ext or logo.ext; it exists only at show level, as there is no season-level clear logo.
Use PNG for clear logos so the alpha channel keeps the surrounding area transparent.
Additional clear logos are named clearlogo-X.ext or logo-X.ext, where X is a number.

A season poster is an image placed inside that season's folder, named with the literal word Season immediately followed by the season number with no space and no separator, then a supported image extension.
For a Specials season the poster base name is the literal string season-specials-poster instead of SeasonXX.
The words Season and Specials inside these filenames must be the English words, regardless of the language of the content.
Additional season posters append a single lowercase alphabetic letter directly after the season number, progressing a, b, c.
Series background art (fanart) is an image in the show folder whose base name is exactly one of: art, backdrop, background, or fanart.
Additional background images are named Custom_Fanart_Name-X.ext, where X is a number.
Square art, used as the details-screen background on the iOS and Android apps, is an image in the show folder whose base name is exactly one of: square, squareArt, or backgroundSquare.
A show banner is an image in the show folder named exactly banner plus a supported image extension.
Additional show banners are named banner-X.ext, where X is a number.
A season banner is an image inside the season folder named with the word Season, then the season number with no space, then the literal suffix -banner, then a supported image extension.
For a Specials season the banner base name is the literal string season-specials-banner.
Additional season banners append a single lowercase alphabetic letter directly after -banner, progressing a, b, c.
Episode artwork is an image file whose name is identical to the episode media file's name apart from the extension, placed in the same folder as the episode file.
A show theme song is an MP3 file named exactly theme.mp3 placed in the main show directory, not in a season folder.
An external subtitle file is named after the episode file, then a dot, then the language code, then the subtitle extension, and is placed in the season folder alongside the episode.
The language code segment of a subtitle filename must be an ISO-639-1 two-letter code or an ISO-639-2/B three-letter code.
External subtitle files are fully supported, meaning compatible with all Plex apps including transcoding clients, in SRT, SMI, and SSA (or ASS) formats.

In a Movie library using the current "Plex Movie" agent, an optional database ID matching hint is written as an opening curly brace, the source keyword, one ASCII hyphen (U+002D), the ID, and a closing curly brace: {source-id}; the only documented movie sources are `imdb` and `tmdb`.

The movie ID hint is appended after the `MovieName (release year)` component, separated by a single space, and the documented example applies the identical hint to both the per-movie folder name and the media filename (the extension follows the closing brace).

The ID portion is the provider's own identifier reproduced as published: an IMDb hint keeps the `tt` prefix and IMDb's own leading zeros (tt0372784), while a TMDB hint is the bare integer with no padding (272); the page states no zero-padding or fixed-width rule of Plex's own.
A movie file must be named `MovieName (release year).ext`, with the four-digit release year in round parentheses immediately after the title, separated from the title by a single space.

Placing each movie in its own folder named identically to the movie file (minus the extension) is the recommended layout: /Movies/MovieName (release year)/MovieName (release year).ext; flat stand-alone movie files directly under the library root are supported but not recommended.

An edition is expressed as a second curly-brace tag of the form {edition-Edition Name} (literal keyword `edition`, one hyphen, then free text up to 32 characters); it requires Plex Pass and the non-legacy Plex Movie agent on Plex Media Server v1.28.1 or newer.

The edition tag and the {source-id} tag may both appear on the same movie, and the order of curly-brace tags relative to each other is not significant; Plex recommends repeating edition info in both folder name and filename.

A movie split across files must live in its own folder and each part is named `MovieName (release year) - Split_Name.ext` where Split_Name is one of cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX or ptX with X replaced by the part number; maximum 8 parts, all parts the same container.

In a TV library using the "Plex TV Series" agent, an optional show ID hint is placed in the SERIES FOLDER name inside curly braces as {tmdb-NNNNNN}, {tvdb-NNNNNN} or {imdb-ttNNNNNN}; the IMDb form carries the `tt` prefix, TMDB and TVDB forms are bare integers.
The TV ID hint belongs on the top-level series folder only; in Plex's own worked example the season folders and the episode filenames beneath it carry no ID hint.
For the Plex TV Series agent, include the four-digit series year in round parentheses after the series title in both the folder name and the episode filenames.
examples: /TV Shows/Band of Brothers (2001)/Season 01/Band of Brothers (2001) - s01e01 - Currahee.mkv

rules.rule: Season-based episodes must carry the notation sXXeXX in the filename (lowercase s and e in every documented example, two digits each), and the separator between the show name, the sXXeXX token and the title may be a dash, a dot or a space.
examples: Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s01e02 - The First Cut is the Deepest.avi

rules.rule: Season directories must use the literal English word "Season" followed by a space and the season number (two digits in every example), regardless of the content's language.
Specials are season zero: the folder must be named either `Season 00` or `Specials`, and the episodes use the s00eXX notation.
examples: /TV Shows/Grey's Anatomy (2005)/Season 00/Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s00e01 - Straight to the Heart.mkv

rules.rule: A single file covering several consecutive episodes is named with the range form sXXeYY-eZZ, giving the first and last episode covered.
Date-based shows put the air date in place of the sXXeXX token, in either YYYY-MM-DD or DD-MM-YYYY order, with dashes, periods or spaces as the internal separator.

Trailing Optional_Info is fed to the Plex TV Series agent as a matching hint, so any text that should NOT influence matching (quality, source, release group) must be wrapped in SQUARE brackets [ ], not curly braces.

An episode split across files is named `ShowName - sXXeYY - Split_Name.ext` where Split_Name is one of cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX or ptX; maximum 8 parts, identical container and stream order across parts.

As an alternative to a folder-name hint, a TV series can be pinned with a `.plexmatch` text file carrying the hint names `tvdbid`, `tmdbid` or `imdbid` (case-insensitive) in `name: value` form; these override title, year and the series directory name, and the imdbid value may be given with or without the `tt` prefix.
A `.plexmatch` file may instead carry a `guid` hint holding a Plex URI-style identifier in the form [source]://[id].

The hint file must be named exactly `.plexmatch` (no extension), placed in a series directory (where it also affects subdirectories) or a season directory; it is line-delimited, leading/trailing whitespace is ignored, blank lines and lines starting with # are comments, and each directive is `hintName: value` with the colon immediately after the name.
Movie content and TV content must live under separate library root paths; the library content location for TV is the folder that directly contains the individual show folders.

Keep each major content type in its own dedicated folder tree. The folder you register as a Movie library's content location must contain movie content only, with no TV, music, or other content type under that same path. That folder does not have to sit at the filesystem root: in Plex's own example it is /Media/Movies, alongside /Media/TV Shows and /Media/Music. It is the main folder of each content type (e.g. /Movies, /Music, /TV Shows) that you specify as the content location for that library type. Plex states its scanners and metadata agents "will only work correctly" when the major content types are separated; mixing movie and television content under one path can cause incorrect matching, poorly classified content, and some files being ignored entirely.

The directory specified as a TV library's content location should be a directory that directly contains the individual show folders, not a show folder itself. That directory is normally the top-level content-type folder (e.g. /TV Shows), but it can be a nested category folder when shows are grouped: with /TV Shows/Kids/ShowName vs /TV Shows/Regular/ShowName, /TV Shows/Kids is the source location for a separate "kids" TV library. (Plex phrases this as what you "would typically specify" rather than a hard technical constraint.)
examples: /TV Shows/Kids  <- content location for a separate "kids" library

rules.rule: Name the show folder as the series title followed by a space and the four-digit release year in parentheses, and repeat that same 'Title (Year)' string at the start of each episode filename.
examples: /Band of Brothers (2001)/Season 01/Band of Brothers (2001) - s01e01 - Currahee.mkv
/Doctor Who (1963)/Season 01/Doctor Who (1963) - s01e01 - An Unearthly Child (1).mp4

rules.rule: When a season directory is used, it must be named with the English word "Season" followed by the season number, even if the content is in another language. Plex's own examples always capitalize "Season" and zero-pad to two digits (Season 01, Season 02, Season 08), though the page does not explicitly state that padding is mandatory. Season-zero content ("specials") is the only exception to the "Season" wording: it goes in a folder named either "Season 00" or "Specials". A miniseries always uses "Season 01".
Zero-pad the season number in the folder name to two digits; the page never states padding as a requirement, but every season folder it shows is two digits.

Every episode filename must carry the season-and-episode token in the form sXXeYY, where XX is the season number and YY is the episode number; this token is the only part of the filename that Plex requires.
Treat everything in the filename other than the sXXeYY token as non-essential for matching; the number pair, read as two-digit season then two-digit episode, is what determines the match.
examples: From the Earth to the Moon (1998) - s01e02.mp4 (no episode title at all)

rules.rule: The delimiter between name components may be a dash, a period, or a space; Plex does not require any specific one, and the page's own worked examples use a plain ASCII hyphen surrounded by single spaces (" - ").
examples: Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s01e02 - The First Cut is the Deepest.avi

rules.rule: Trailing extra information is optional; put it in square brackets [ ] if you want the Plex TV Series agent to ignore it, because unbracketed trailing text is fed into the agent as a matching hint.
examples: Bracket a fansub or release-group tag so it is not treated as a title hint: ShowName (2020) - s01e01 - Episode Title [SubGroup][1080p].mkv

rules.rule: To pin the match, append the provider ID to the show folder name inside curly braces using exactly the prefixes tmdb-, tvdb-, or imdb-tt: {tmdb-123456}, {tvdb-123456}, {imdb-tt123456}.

Plex frames anime absolute numbering purely as an episode-ordering choice, not as a distinct on-disk layout: handling an anime series as a single season is described as something some users elect to do using "Absolute" series order.
examples: This is the ONLY sentence about anime on the page; it prescribes no folder or filename format of its own.

rules.rule: The library's Episode Ordering setting must be set to whichever database your files were numbered from; the default for the Plex TV Series agent is TMDB aired order, and it is changed under the Advanced tab when creating or editing the TV library.
examples: Secondary official source (https://support.plex.tv/articles/advanced-setting-plex-tv-series-agent/) states the setting's meaning verbatim: "Episode Ordering: How episodes are named/numbered on disk. If your naming follows The MovieDB or TheTVDB choose that here."

rules.rule: From Plex Media Server 1.40.4 onward, with the Plex TV Series agent, set the episode order per show (not just per library) from the Advanced tab when editing that show, and only after the show has been matched.
examples: Edit show > Advanced tab > Episode ordering
If an order is missing, refresh metadata; orders created within roughly 48 hours may be incomplete

rules.rule: "TheTVDB (Absolute)" is one of the selectable episode-ordering values, alongside The Movie Database (Aired), TheTVDB (Aired), and TheTVDB (DVD); select it for an anime numbered by absolute order.

Specials belong to season zero. Place them in a folder directly under the show folder named either "Season 00" or "Specials" (the page names these two forms and says nothing about other variants or case), and number the files s00e<episode> with a two-digit episode number, as in "/TV Shows/ShowName/Specials/ShowName - s00e13 - Optional_Info.ext" and "/TV Shows/Grey's Anatomy (2005)/Season 00/Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s00e01 - Straight to the Heart.mkv". Take the episode number from TMDB's listing for that special rather than assigning your own; if unsure whether an episode is a special, check it on TMDB and name it as shown there. If the item does not appear on TMDB at all (DVD special, behind the scenes, goof reel), do not give it an s00e number: add it as an "extra" for the show instead, per the Plex TV extras article.
examples: /Grey's Anatomy (2005)/Season 00/Grey's Anatomy (2005) - s00e01 - Straight to the Heart.mkv
Relevant to anime OVAs and specials, though the page never says so

rules.rule: An extra-like item that does not exist as a special on TMDB should be added as a show "extra" rather than numbered into season 00.
examples: Creditless openings/endings and behind-the-scenes reels would fall here, but the page names only "DVD special, behind the scenes, goof reel"

rules.rule: A single file covering several consecutive episodes is named sXXeYY-eZZ, giving the first and last episode covered, with the second episode number prefixed by a lowercase 'e' and joined by a hyphen.
A miniseries uses the ordinary season layout with the season always fixed at 01.
examples: /From the Earth to the Moon (1998)/Season 01/From the Earth to the Moon (1998) - s01e01.mp4

rules.rule: One episode split across several files keeps the same sXXeYY token and ends with one of the part suffixes cdX, discX, diskX, dvdX, partX, or ptX, numbered from 1, with a maximum of 8 parts and identical format and stream layout across parts.
examples: Only stacks up to 8 parts are supported

rules.rule: Date-based shows are shown inside a Season folder, with the sXXeXX marker replaced by the air date: /TV Shows/ShowName/Season NN/ShowName - DATE - Optional_Info.ext (the page's templates write \"Season 02\" as a placeholder; the worked example uses Season 08, so use the show's actual season number). The date may be in either YYYY-MM-DD or DD-MM-YYYY order, and its internal separator may be a dash (2011-11-15), a period (2011.11.15) or a space (2011 11 15). The delimiter surrounding the date is separate from that internal separator: the page's templates use a spaced en dash and its concrete example uses a spaced hyphen, as in /TV Shows/The Colbert Report (2005)/Season 08/The Colbert Report (2005) - 2011-11-15 - Elijah Wood.avi. Note the page shows every date-based example inside a Season folder but never states in words that the folder is mandatory.
examples: /The Colbert Report (2005)/Season 08/The Colbert Report (2005) - 2011-11-15 - Elijah Wood.avi

rules.rule: Rather than renaming oddly numbered files, a .plexmatch file in the series or season directory can carry Pattern hints whose {curly brace} match tokens (s/se/season, e/ep/episode, sp/special, see) accept a validity range [start]-[end], an offset +N or -N, and a max digit length lN, remapping the numbers parsed from filenames onto the numbers Plex should use.
examples: see indicates a combined season and episode number (e.g. "214" would refer to season 2, episode 14), from PMS 1.30.2
Source: https://support.plex.tv/articles/plexmatch/ (secondary official page; it never mentions anime)

rules.rule: A .plexmatch file can also pin one file at a time with 'ep: <number>: <filename>', where the number is SP[X], E[X] or bare [X], or S[X]E[Y], optionally with a hyphenated range, and the hint overrides any number parsed from the filename, directory name, or season hint.
Treat .ext in every documented pattern as a placeholder for the file's real container extension, not a literal.
